## Hexagonal Revetment Block Mould Buyer Guide

Revetment block moulds are specified as side length × block height, plus wall thickness. Wall thickness is the durability decision and is usually tapered so blocks release cleanly from the mould.

## How to specify a revetment block mould

- Side length 14.5–18cm: lighter mats for canal linings, garden slopes and low-flow banks.

- Side length 20cm: the most widely used revetment size — 25 designs available with heights from 6cm to 30cm.

- Side length 22–25cm: heavy revetment for main river banks and high-flow channels.

- Wall thickness 3–8.7cm: quoted as a taper such as 6–5cm, meaning 6cm at the wide face and 5cm at the narrow face for clean demoulding.

## Project drawing checklist

For revetment block moulds, wall thickness and block height together decide concrete volume per square metre. Send the slope drawing or design specification and we can match the closest catalogue mould.

- Confirm side length and block height (e.g. 20×15cm).

- State required wall thickness, including taper if specified (e.g. 6–5cm).

- Tell us whether the core is planted with grass or filled with gravel.

ApplicationSuitable mould typeKey parameters

Canal & garden slope lining14.5–18cm hollow hexagon blocksSide length, height, wall thickness
River bank & embankment20cm hollow hexagon blocksHeight, wall thickness taper, core opening
High-flow channel & reservoir22–25cm hollow hexagon blocksSide length, height, wall thickness, edge units

## Hollow Hexagon Block Mould FAQ

## What is a hexagonal revetment block used for?
Hollow hexagonal revetment blocks are laid across river banks, canal slopes and highway embankments. They interlock on six sides to resist water flow, and their open cores are planted with grass or filled with gravel so the slope becomes vegetated erosion control.

## What does wall thickness 6–5cm mean?
It is a tapered wall: 6cm at the wide face and 5cm at the narrow face. The taper lets the cast block release cleanly from the mould and is standard practice on hollow revetment blocks.

## How do I choose the right revetment block size?
Side length 14.5–18cm suits canal linings and low-flow banks, 20cm is the most widely used size for river banks and embankments, and 22–25cm is specified for high-flow channels and main river works. Block height then follows the design concrete volume.

## Do you supply half-hexagon blocks for the mat edge?
Yes. We supply hollow half-hexagon and semi-hollow moulds in 15×20, 17×8, 20×6, 20×8, 20×12, 20×15, 20×40×12 and 25×20cm so the revetment mat can be finished at the edge without cutting blocks.

## Moulds for Concrete Hollow Blocks and Hollow Bricks
Hollow block moulds — also called concrete block making moulds or hollow bricks moulds — are used to cast the cored masonry units that form walls, partitions, boundary walls and ventilated screens. Because the core geometry decides both block weight and mortar key, hole shape and wall thickness are the two parameters buyers check first.

## Hollow Block Mould Buyer Guide

Hollow block mould selection is driven by finished block size, hole geometry and how many blocks you need per pour. Multi-cavity ABS moulds cut labour per block but need a flatter casting bed.

## Typical hollow block mould types

- ABS three-in-one multi-cavity: casts three 20×20×10cm blocks per pour with double-smooth faces — the fastest option for volume production.

- Double-sided S30 series: 22 pattern designs in 30×30×10cm, finished on both faces so blocks can be laid either way round.

- Numbered 20×20cm designs: No.20-14 to No.20-28 plus No.104/105/106/109 — established patterns with proven demoulding.

- Square, round & angled hole: core geometry chosen for block weight, mortar key and whether rebar passes through.

## Project drawing checklist

For hollow block moulds, the key parameters are finished block dimensions, hole shape and wall thickness between cores. Tell us your target blocks-per-day and we can advise on cavity count.

- Confirm finished block length × width × height (e.g. 20×20×10cm).

- State hole shape, hole count and minimum wall thickness between cores.

- Tell us target output per day so we can recommend single or multi-cavity moulds.

## Hollow Block Mould FAQ

## What is a hollow block mould used for?
A hollow block mould casts concrete masonry units with internal cores. The cores reduce block weight, save concrete, improve insulation and give mortar a mechanical key. Blocks are used for boundary walls, partitions and ventilated screens.

## How many blocks can one mould cast per pour?
Single-cavity moulds cast one block per pour. Our ABS three-in-one moulds cast three blocks per pour and two-in-one moulds cast two, which significantly reduces labour cost per block.

## What is the difference between a hollow block and a solid block mould?
A hollow block mould has core formers that create internal voids, so the finished unit is lighter and uses less concrete. A solid block mould produces a fully filled unit with higher compressive strength but more weight and material cost.

## Can you make a custom hollow block mould from my drawing?
Yes. Send the block drawing or a sample photo with finished dimensions, hole layout and wall thickness. We review draft angles and demoulding direction, then quote OEM mould production.

## Hollow & Interlocking Slope Block Mould Buyer Guide

These 10 moulds all produce blocks that key into their neighbours, but the keying mechanism differs — and that mechanism, not the block size, is what determines whether the slope holds.

## Four keying mechanisms, four use cases

- Tongue-and-groove interlocking: straight ribs and slots on the block edges. Simple to lay, resists sliding down-slope.

- Dovetail interlocking: wedge-shaped joints that cannot be pulled apart in-plane. Specified where uplift or wave action is a concern.

- Locking blocks: square 43 × 43 × 10 cm format that keys on all four sides for a uniform grid.

- Hollow ecological blocks: open grass-planting voids plus interlocking edges, so the slope both vegetates and stays keyed.

## Three things buyers get wrong

- Treating "interlocking" and "dovetail" as the same product. They are not interchangeable: a dovetail joint resists being pulled apart, a plain tongue-and-groove joint mainly resists sliding. Confirm which one your design requires before comparing prices.

- Quoting from the outer size when the interlock adds to it. The tongue projects beyond the block body. Two blocks both described as "40 × 34 cm" can have different overall mould footprints depending on how the interlock is measured.

- Underestimating demoulding on deep interlocks and voids. Deep dovetails and open grass-planting cells are the highest-risk features for demoulding damage. This is a real production constraint — plan release agent and demould timing, and expect it to affect achievable cycles per day.

Slope conditionSuitable blockKey parameters

General slope, resist slidingTongue-and-groove interlocking blockFace size, thickness, rib depth
Wave action / uplift riskDovetail interlocking blockDovetail geometry, thickness
Uniform grid, all-side keyingSquare locking blockBlock size, keying on four sides
Slope requiring vegetationHollow ecological blockOpen void ratio, cell size

The hollow area can support vegetation or drainage while the concrete frame helps protect the slope from erosion.

## Kerbstone & Side Stone Mould Buyer Guide

48 qualified moulds across 16 profile families, from 20 cm corner pieces to 50 cm straight runs. Slope and S-type profiles are the volume products; corner and elbow pieces exist so a kerb line can actually turn.

## The six profile families

- Slope kerbstone (10 sizes): the workhorse. 35×35, 49×18 up to 50×20×20 cm. A sloped top face sheds water toward the carriageway.

- S-type kerbstone (10 sizes): curved S face, 30×29 to 50×35 cm. Used where a softer transition between road and footway is wanted.

- L-type kerbstone (4 sizes): right-angle section, 25×20 to 49.5×36 cm. Also available with a flat outer edge.

- Curved kerbstone (4 sizes): radius units for bends and islands, including a 20×30×15 cm angled integrated profile.

- Line-profile kerbstone (4 sizes): flat-faced with a recessed line, 30×30×12 to 50×15×6 cm.

- Chamfered & angled (5 sizes): bevelled top arris, 50×10×10 to 50×12×15.5 cm.

## Three things buyers get wrong

- “50 × 35 × 18–7” is not a tolerance. On slope and S-type kerbs the last pair is the height at each end of the same unit — 18 cm at the high end, 7 cm at the low end. That taper is the drainage fall built into the kerb. Read as a tolerance band you will order a mould that cannot produce your channel gradient, so always confirm which end your drawing dimension refers to.

- A corner marked “30–30” means outer and inner arc length. Same convention as our power coping corners: the two figures are the outside and inside face of one curved piece, not length by width. Corner and elbow units must also be ordered in the same profile family as the straight runs, or the faces will not line up at the joint.

- “1-out-2” changes your unit price maths. The 50×13×10 cm water-barrier mould casts two pieces per pour. When you compare quotations, check whether the price is per finished kerb or per mould — a 1-out-2 tool at twice the price is the same cost per unit, with half the cycle time.

## Specifying a kerb line, not just a kerb

Kerbs are bought by the run, and a run is never all straight. Working out the corner and transition pieces before quoting avoids a second shipment later.

- Count straight metres first, then every bend, and note the radius of each.

- For each bend decide whether it is served by a curved unit or by a corner/elbow piece — we hold both.

- Drainage inlets need the S-type drainage kerb (49.5×29×20 cm) with its notch and hole; count these separately.

- Where the kerb line ends at a barrier or island, the traffic separator mould (50×35×50 cm, Ø5 cm hole) finishes it.

- Confirm whether your project measures kerb height from the channel or from the finished footway level.

## Production notes

Kerbs are high-volume repeat castings, so demoulding behaviour matters more than on one-off components.

- Sloped and chamfered top faces carry the visible arris — ABS holds that edge sharper over many cycles.

- Long 50 cm units benefit from a stiffer wall to stay straight when handled wet.

- Typical service life is 150+ pour cycles with normal demoulding practice.

- Send a section drawing rather than a product name: two kerbs called “slope kerb” can differ by 10 cm in width.

## Kerbstone, curbstone, side stone — one product, many names

These are regional names for the same precast road-edge unit, not different products:

- Kerbstone / kerb mould (British English) and curbstone / curb mold (American English) are the same word.

- Road curb, side stone, road edge stone and concrete kerb all refer to this product family.

- Match the cross-section profile, not the name — send a drawing or section photo if your local term is not listed here.

## Radius Kerbs — Casting a Curve, Not a Straight Line

Moulds marked R1000 and 1/3: a 1 metre radius curve, divided into thirds. A curved kerb line is never one bent unit — the arc is split into segments, and each segment must be tapered (shorter on the inner face than the outer) so the joints close evenly. Cast a curve from rectangular blocks and you get a wedge-shaped gap at every joint. One mould equals one radius, so tell us the radius your drawing calls for.

## Kerbstone Mould FAQ

## What does a size like “50 × 35 × 18–7 cm” mean on a kerbstone mould?
The last pair is the height at the two ends of the same kerb: 18 cm at the high end and 7 cm at the low end. That taper is the drainage fall designed into the unit, not a tolerance or a size range. Tell us which end your drawing dimension refers to so the gradient comes out right.

## How do I read the two figures on a curved or corner unit?
They are the outer and inner arc length of one piece, the same convention we use on power coping corners. A “30–30” corner measures 30 cm along both faces; it is not 30 by 30 cm in plan.

## Do corner pieces work with any straight kerb?
No. Corner and elbow units must come from the same profile family as the straight runs, otherwise the visible faces will not align at the joint. We hold chamfered, line-profile and curved-angled corners specifically so each family can turn.

## What does “1-out-2” mean for pricing?
It means the mould casts two finished pieces per pour. The 50×13×10 cm water-barrier mould is 1-out-2, so when comparing quotations check whether the price is per finished kerb or per mould — the cost per unit and the cycle time are what actually differ.

## Which profile should I choose for a standard road kerb?
Slope and S-type cover most road work: slope for a straightforward shed toward the channel, S-type where a softer road-to-footway transition is wanted. L-type suits raised edges and planting beds. Send a section drawing, since two kerbs both called “slope kerb” can differ by 10 cm in width.

## Do you have moulds for drainage inlets in the kerb line?
Yes. The S-type drainage kerb is 49.5×29×20 cm with a 12×1.5 cm notch and a Ø4.2–3 cm hole. Count inlet units separately from the straight run when you send quantities.

## PP or ABS for kerbstone moulds?
ABS where the top arris is chamfered or sloped and must stay sharp across many cycles; PP for plain high-volume production. Both give 150+ pour cycles with normal demoulding practice.

## Are kerbstone moulds the same as curbstone molds?
Yes. Kerbstone (British English) and curbstone (American English) are the same precast concrete road-edge unit; mould and mold are the same word spelled differently. Road curb, side stone, road edge stone and concrete kerb usually refer to the same product family. Always confirm the cross-section profile rather than the name, because regional standards differ.

## Can you make a mould for our local road-authority kerb profile?
Yes. OEM tooling from a cross-section drawing or sample is standard for municipal projects that must follow a local authority profile. A drawing is preferred; clear photos of the section plus finished dimensions are enough for an initial feasibility review. Straight and radius pieces of the same custom profile can both be produced.

## What is the MOQ and lead time for kerbstone moulds?
Standard catalogue profiles have no strict MOQ and mixed-SKU orders are welcome; OEM profiles depend on profile complexity. Lead time is typically 15–30 days after drawing approval. Send your profile, quantities and destination port for an FOB Ningbo/Shanghai quote.

## Manhole Cover Mould Buyer Guide

Cover moulds are quoted on finished slab size, not on the mould's outer size. Read this before sending an enquiry.

## Cover only, or cover plus frame?

This is the single most common source of re-quoting. A cover slab cast on its own will not sit flush unless the surrounding frame was cast from a matching mould with the correct seat clearance.

- Cover only: you already have steel or existing concrete frames on site.

- Cover + frame set: two moulds, dimensioned together so the cover drops into the seat. The 50 × 50 cm square set on this page is an example.

- Frame only: the Ø 68 × 10 cm round frame mould gives a Ø 61 cm clear opening — the opening, not the outer diameter, is what has to match your shaft.

## Two dimensions buyers usually get wrong

- Round covers are quoted by diameter, thickness second. Ø 80 × 5.5 cm means an 80 cm circle 5.5 cm deep. A 5.5 cm slab is a pedestrian / light-duty cover; it is not a roadway load-class part unless your own concrete design and reinforcement say so.

- Drainage-hole dimensions are the slot, not the pitch. On the five-hole Ø 80 cm cover the openings are Ø 22 × 4 and Ø 20 × 3 — those are the cast void sizes. If your local standard fixes the hole pattern, send the drawing; hole layout is the cheapest thing to change before tooling and the most expensive after.

We do not publish load classes for this category. Load class is a property of your finished concrete mix and reinforcement, not of the plastic mould, and quoting one would be misleading.

## Manhole Cover Mould FAQ

## Do I need the frame mould as well as the cover mould?
Only if you are casting the frame in concrete too. If your site already has steel frames or existing concrete seats, the cover mould alone is enough — but send the seat opening size so the cover is dimensioned to drop into it. Where both parts are cast, order them as a matched set so the seat clearance is designed in.

## What load class do these covers achieve?
We do not quote a load class, because it is not a property of the plastic mould. Load capacity comes from your concrete mix, reinforcement and slab thickness. The 6 cm and 5.5 cm covers here are typical pedestrian and light-utility sections; for trafficked covers, design your own reinforcement and tell us the finished thickness you need.

## Can the mould include a logo or utility marking text?
Yes. Logo, lettering, utility name and anti-slip surface patterns can be tooled into the cover from drawings or clear sample photos. Markings are fixed before the mould is cut, so send the artwork with the enquiry.

## Should I quote the finished cover size or the mould's outer size?
Always quote the finished slab size you need the cured concrete cover to be — diameter, or length × width, then thickness. The dimensions on this page (such as 50 × 50 × 6 cm and Ø 80 × 5.5 cm) are finished cover dimensions, not the mould's outer dimensions. We size the mould around your finished slab, including the small draft allowance for demoulding.

## Can you make a cover mould that fits my existing frame?
Yes. For an existing steel or concrete frame, measure the clear seat opening and the cover thickness it accepts, and send a photo or drawing. We dimension the cover to drop into that seat with the correct clearance. If you also need to cast the frame, order the cover and frame as a matched set so the seat is designed together.

## Shaft Brick Mould Buyer Guide

Three numbers decide whether a ring closes: inner diameter, brick width and pieces per course. They have to come from the same drawing.

## One mould equals one diameter

Each ring brick mould is cut to a single arc. That arc is what makes the course close into a true circle, and it is why the piece count is not a choice:

- Ø 70 cm — 7 bricks per course, 17.5 cm wide

- Ø 80 cm — 8 bricks per course, 18.5 cm wide

- Ø 90 cm — 9 bricks per course

- Ø 110 cm — 11 bricks per course, 24 cm wide

- Ø 130 cm — 23.5 cm wide (R65)

- Ø 150 cm — 24 cm wide (R75)

A Ø 90 cm mould will not build a Ø 110 cm shaft. If your project mixes diameters, you need one mould per diameter — that is normal, and mixed-SKU shipments are standard for us.

## Inner diameter is not excavation width

Every diameter on this page is the inner diameter — the clear bore a worker climbs down. The outer diameter is the inner figure plus twice the brick width:

- Ø 110 cm bore + 2 × 24 cm walls ≈ 158 cm outer

- Ø 70 cm bore + 2 × 17.5 cm walls ≈ 105 cm outer

Trench and shoring width comes from the outer figure. Buyers who size excavation from the bore end up short by roughly half a metre on the large diameters.

## Course height and reinforcement

Ring bricks here are 20 cm high, so a 3 m deep shaft is 15 courses. We do not publish load or depth ratings: those depend on your concrete mix, any vertical reinforcement threaded through the wall, and the surrounding backfill — not on the plastic mould.

## Shaft Ring & Well Wall Brick Mould FAQ

## How many ring bricks do I need per course, and how is that decided?
It is fixed by the mould, not by you on site. Each ring brick mould is cut to one arc, so a Ø 70 cm shaft takes 7 bricks per course, Ø 80 cm takes 8, Ø 90 cm takes 9 and Ø 110 cm takes 11. The pieces only close into a circle at their own diameter, so a Ø 90 cm mould cannot be used to build a Ø 110 cm shaft.

## Is the diameter you quote the inner diameter or the outer diameter?
Inner diameter — the clear bore of the finished shaft. Add twice the brick width for the outer size: a Ø 110 cm shaft with 24 cm wide bricks measures about 158 cm across the outside. Excavation width is sized from the outer figure, so always confirm which one your drawing uses before ordering.

## What is the difference between shaft ring bricks and well wall bricks?
Ring bricks are curved segments for circular shafts and only fit one diameter. Well wall bricks are straight rectangular units, used for square or rectangular inspection chambers and for straight wall runs; the 30 x 15 x 17.3 cm unit has a tongue and groove so courses interlock, and the 32 x 18 x 17.3 cm corner brick turns the corner while keeping the same course height.

## Can you make ring brick moulds for a diameter that is not listed?
Yes. Give us the inner diameter, the wall thickness you want and the course height, and we set the arc and the piece count so the ring closes exactly. Odd diameters are routine work; what matters is that all three figures come from the same drawing.

## Notched Cover Mould Buyer Guide

The notch is a designed edge cut for a crossing service — quote its size and position. Pick thickness by the load on top and the surface/function variant by whether the trench carries cables or water.

## Five cover groups on this page

- Standard notched (36): 6–12cm covers for cable trenches and light/medium roadside ditches, 25–75cm.

- Heavy-duty / deep (12): 12–20cm sections for main-roadside load and deep U-channels; several in ABS.

- Recessed / dished (9): tray-top 凹面 covers for flush paving infill or water flow; deep 12–18cm highway pieces.

- Variants (6): striped & dot-pattern tops, 6-hole perforated, square-hole service opening, double-notch junction covers.

- Highway / project (9): Laibin-Du'an, Pingyi, Guizhou highway/transport authority and Gandong College covers.

## Three things buyers get wrong

- Cutting the notch on site after casting. A notch cut into a finished cover breaks the edge and loses the piece — order the notch moulded (quote width × depth and middle/end position).

- Ordering a standard 6–8cm cover for a main-roadside trench. Vehicle-load trenches need the 12–20cm heavy/deep covers, often ABS; thickness and reinforcement set load, the notch does not weaken the span.

- Mismatching the cover and U-channel seat. Covers pair with a specific channel (e.g. 50×30×10 cover sits a 50×30.9×20 U-channel). Order both moulds together and confirm seat dimensions so the cover sits flush.

ApplicationCover type & typical thicknessQuote details to prepare

Cable trench (services branch off)Standard notched, 6–10cmL×W×T, notch W×D, notch position (middle/end)

Main-roadside ditch, vehicle loadHeavy/deep notched, 12–20cm (ABS for thick)L×W×T, load class, notch, matching U-channel seat

Water-carrying trench6-hole perforated or square-holeHole size/count, flow, L×W×T

## Notched Drainage Cover Mould 80×49×15 cm — Ribbed Back Structure

A flat 80 cm cover warps without the back rib grid — always check rib layout on any cover over ~60 cm. An 80 cm outer cover suits roughly a 65–70 cm clear span; the rest is bearing on both trench walls.

## Notched Drainage Cover Mould FAQ

## What is a notched (slotted) drainage cover mould?
It is a plastic (PP/ABS) injection mould for a concrete trench or ditch cover that has a notch cut into one edge (缺口). The notch is not damage — it is designed so that a pipe or cable can cross the trench at that cover position: the cover drops over the crossing line instead of the pipe having to go under or through the concrete. These covers are standard on cable trenches, roadside ditches and utility channels where service lines branch off. Quote the notch size (width × depth, e.g. 20×1.5cm, 30×1.5cm) and its position.

## Where does the notch go — middle of a run or at the end?
Two cases are common. A middle / inline notch sits on the edge of a cover mid-trench, where a pipe crosses between two cover runs. An end notch is on the last cover of a run where the service exits the trench end. Some trenches also need a double-notched cover (e.g. 59×54×10) where a pipe crosses at a junction or two lines meet. Tell us where the crossing falls; a site-cut notch after casting breaks the cover edge and voids the piece.

## Standard vs heavy-duty / deep notched covers — how to choose?
Standard covers run 6–12cm thick for cable trenches and light/medium roadside ditches. Heavy / deep covers run 12–20cm (e.g. 50×50×18, 59×50×18, 60×49×20, 63×36×15, 58×40×15 ABS) for main-roadside trenches subject to vehicle load and for deep U-channels. The very deep 15–20cm pieces are often specified in ABS for stiffness and to hold the thick section straight. Load class is set by thickness and reinforcement, not by the notch; the notch itself is kept clear of the load-bearing edge.

## What is a recessed / dished (凹面) notched cover?
A recessed or dished cover has a shallow tray formed in the top surface rather than a flat top. Two uses: the tray can be filled with paving/grate infill to sit flush with a footpath or plaza, or it sheds/collects water for a drain that takes flow. Dished covers are typically deeper sections (12–18cm, e.g. 26×24×12, 39×24×12, 59×50×18, 65×36×16, 69×36×16, 75×49×15.3) and many are made for highway and transport-authority projects. The 凹底 (recessed-bottom) 75×30×10 is the inverse: a formed bottom for a specific channel seat.

## Striped, dot-pattern, 6-hole and square-hole variants — what are they for?
These are surface/function variants of the notched cover: striped and dot-pattern tops add slip resistance and a finished look on pedestrian-accessible trenches (e.g. striped 59×50×10 and 74×50×10, dot 61×49×3.2); 6-hole covers (e.g. 40×30×6) perforate the slab for stormwater flow where the trench drains surface water; square-hole covers (71×49×8) have a large formed service opening for a bigger pipe or chamber access. Choose by whether the trench carries cables (solid notched) or water (perforated) and the walking-surface requirement.

## Can you make highway-project and custom notched covers?
Yes — much of this range is project tooling made to highway and institutional drawings. The catalogue includes Laibin-Du'an expressway (来都高速, 65×49×10 and 75×49×10), Pingyi expressway (平益高速, 69.5×49.5×10 and dished 75×49×14), Guizhou highway/transport-authority (贵州高速/贵州交投, 60×49×16, 70×50×8, 75×49×15.3) and Gandong College (赣东学院, 67×50×6.5) covers. For your own project send the cover L×W×T, the notch size and position, the surface type (plain/striped/dot/perforated), the load/application and any standard it must meet; we confirm mould design and demoulding.

## Does the notch weaken the cover, and is there a mould for the matching U-channel?
The notch is a small edge cut (typically 1.5–3cm deep across an 8–20cm-thick slab) kept away from the main span, so it does not govern load capacity; heavy covers are simply thicker. Many notched covers pair with a one-piece U-channel — for example the 50×30×10 cover is noted as pairing with a U-channel 50×30.9×20cm. If you are lining a trench, order the cover mould and the matching channel mould together and we confirm the seat dimensions so the cover (with or without a notch) sits flush.

## Material, MOQ and lead time?
Standard 6–12cm covers in PP give 150+ pour cycles and are the economical choice for cable-trench and municipal runs; deep/heavy 12–20cm and dished highway covers suit ABS for stiffer walls and sharper release. Mixed-SKU orders have no strict MOQ across the 72 catalogue moulds; custom project moulds are made to order in roughly 15–30 days after drawing approval. Send the drawing, cover count and destination port for an FOB Ningbo/Shanghai quote; WhatsApp a photo of the cover you want to match and we confirm the nearest catalogue size.

## Paver Block Mould Buyer Guide

Paver jobs fail on three things: picking a decorative shape for vehicle loads, laying hollow units without the right sub-base, and ignoring pattern direction on four-piece motifs. Get these right and the pavement lasts and looks planned.

## Choosing by application

- Green parking / fire lanes / sponge city: hollow permeable grass-grid hexagons (12.5/5 and 13.5/5.5) or the 48 cm holed slab — fill holes with soil+seed or gravel; build the open-graded sub-base first, otherwise the grass dies and the slab cracks.

- Municipal sidewalks: 25–30 cm square/interlocking colored pavers 5–6 cm thick, plus tactile blister/strip tiles at crossings, stops and hazards (usually bright yellow).

- Community roads / driveways: I/H-shaped and tooth/serrated interlockers 6–8 cm thick — the interlock transfers vehicle loads across joints.

- Plazas, parks, courtyards: shaped (clover, crescent, bow, diamond, arrow) and patterned (maple leaf, plum blossom, chrysanthemum, Spanish, double-fan) decorative tiles — buy by the layout, not by the piece.

- Resurfacing old pavement: thin 2–3 cm overlay pavers bonded onto a sound base — they are veneers, not structural slabs.

## What to get right when ordering

- Solid vs hollow: confirm whether the unit must carry grass/water (hollow) or just pave (solid). Most "colored pavers" are solid; only the permeable hexagons and holed slab in this range are hollow.

- Four-piece motifs: plum blossom, chrysanthemum and other quarter-pattern tiles complete one flower per four tiles — order in multiples of four and fix pouring/laying direction.

- Color: iron-oxide pigment mixed into the concrete; white cement for bright pastels. A pigmented wear-course layer saves pigment cost on thick tiles.

- Cavities change the price: 1-out-9 makes nine tiles per pour — compare per-tile cost and daily output, not per mould.

- Thickness = duty: 4–5 cm for foot traffic, 6 cm for community roads, 8 cm for occasional vehicle loads; don't pave driveways with 3 cm veneers.

## Paver Block Mould FAQ

## What is the difference between a colored paver mould and a permeable/grass paver mould?
A standard colored paver (cai zhuan) mould casts a solid decorative or interlocking concrete tile for sidewalks and plazas. A permeable or grass paver mould casts a hollow unit with through holes: after laying, the holes are filled with soil and grass (or gravel), so the surface stays green while carrying light traffic — typical for parking bays, fire access lanes and sponge-city projects. In this catalogue only the hexagonal units (outer 12.5/13.5 cm with 5/5.5 cm inner holes) and the 48×24×8 cm serrated slab with two through holes are hollow; the shaped and patterned pavers are solid.

## Can I use colored concrete in these moulds, and how is the color made?
Yes — that is why they are called colored paver moulds. Iron-oxide pigment is mixed into the concrete before pouring (or a pigmented wear-course layer is poured first, then the base concrete). Smooth ABS/PP faces release cleanly so the color stays even. White cement gives brighter pastel tones; grey cement with pigment gives deeper reds, yellows and greens.

## How do I read dimensions like 25 x 25 x 5 cm or outer 12.5 / inner 5 cm?
For solid pavers it is length x width x thickness in centimetres. For permeable hexagons, the outer measurement is the hexagon's overall size (opposite-flat distance) and the inner measurement is the planting/drainage hole — a 12.5/5 unit has a 12.5 cm body with a 5 cm hole. Thin 2–3 cm units are overlay/veneer pavers for resurfacing existing pavements, not heavy-duty slabs.

## Which paver shapes are best for driveways versus footways?
For driveways and fire lanes use hollow grass-grid/permeable units (filled and compacted) or thick interlocking I/H-shaped pavers (24–30 cm, 6 cm thick) whose joints transfer load. Footways, plazas and courtyards can use the decorative shaped and patterned pavers — clover, crescent, bow, diamond, maple-leaf and the four-piece flower patterns are designed to be combined into layouts, not to carry vehicle loads.

## Do the four-piece flower patterns (plum blossom, chrysanthemum) come as one mould or four?
Each tile carries one quarter of the motif; four tiles laid together form one complete flower. Order in multiples of four pieces per full motif and plan the layout before pouring so the pattern direction is consistent. The same applies to the Spanish-style and double-fan continuous patterns.

## What are tactile pavers and where are they required?
Tactile (blister/strip) pavers guide visually impaired pedestrians: raised dots (blister/warning tiles) mark hazards, stops and turns; long strips (directional tiles) mark the safe walking line. They are mandatory on municipal sidewalks, stations and public buildings. We supply both types in 20 × 20 × 6 cm and 25 × 25 × 5 cm in PP; color is usually bright yellow.

## What does 1-out-2 or 1-out-9 mean?
It is the number of finished tiles one mould casts per pour — a 1-out-9 rough-stone mould makes nine 10 × 10 cm tiles in a single cycle. More cavities mean lower cost per tile for high-volume items. Compare quotes per finished tile and per daily output, not per mould.

## PP or ABS for colored and decorative paver moulds?
PP (polypropylene) is the default and handles 150+ pour cycles with good flexibility for demoulding. ABS is chosen where deep crisp patterns, sharp arrises or textured faces (rough-stone, fine anti-slip grooves) must stay precise over many cycles — the fine detail releases more sharply in ABS. Tell us the pattern and expected volume and we will recommend the grade.

## What is the MOQ and lead time?
Standard catalogue paver moulds have no strict MOQ and mixed-SKU orders are welcome. Lead time is typically 15–30 days; OEM shapes, logos or custom patterns depend on complexity. Send sizes, quantities and destination port for an FOB Ningbo/Shanghai quote.

# Product: Photovoltaic Pier Moulds
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/products/photovoltaic-pier-moulds

Fixed-tilt & tracker basesCustom bolt patternsEmbed plates accepted150+ pour cycles

## Built for ground-mount and rooftop solar foundations
A photovoltaic pier (also called a PV pile cap, solar foundation block or ballast block) is the precast concrete base that the solar mounting structure bolts or rests on. The mould has to produce a dimensionally consistent block because the post bases or tracker bearings are bolted to it — a few millimetres of error across a few thousand blocks makes installation much slower.
Zhihua supplies PP / ABS plastic moulds for the common flat-pier profiles and builds custom moulds from your foundation drawing. We can cast in bolt pockets, anchor-plate recesses, cable grooves, drainage holes and lifting anchors as part of the mould so the finished block comes out ready for the mounting crew.

Stock sizes30 × 20 × 30 cm and 30 × 30 × 30 cm grooved / plain flat piers. Other sizes are cut to order from your drawing.
Project typesUtility-scale ground-mount farms, commercial rooftop distributed PV, single-axis tracker foundations, agricultural PV (agrivoltaics) and floating-PV shore bases.
What we can cast inBolt pockets (M10–M20 common), cast-in plates, rebar chairs, cable-routing grooves, drainage slots, lifting anchors / holes and project marking.
Material & lifePP for standard piers (150+ pours), ABS when the embed detail is fine and tolerance is tight. Cold-weather and high-abrasion versions available.

## Representative PV Pier Moulds
The two flat-pier profiles we keep in tooling. Custom bolt patterns and embed details can be added to either, or a new mould cut to your foundation section.

## Grooved Flat PV Pier Mould — 30 × 20 × 30 cm
Smaller grooved pier for lightweight support seats and cable routing

## Grooved Flat PV Pier Mould — 30 × 30 × 30 cm
Larger grooved pier with room for a wider support seat and hardware

## Plain Flat PV Pier Mould — 30 × 30 × 30 cm
Simple flat block used as a ballast base or where no groove is required

## The five things that make or break a PV pier order
Solar foundations look simple, but the cost of a wrong mould shows up on site when the mounting crew cannot bolt the posts down. These are the points we check on every drawing before cutting a mould.

- Bolt / embed plate layout. Send the centre-to-centre spacing, thread size (M12 / M16 / M20 are the common ones), projection above the concrete, and whether the hardware is cast-in or post-installed. Cast-in plates and bolt pockets need to be built into the mould, not drilled afterwards.

- Block size vs foundation drawing. The 30 × 30 × 30 cm size is the finished concrete block. The mould is slightly larger to allow for the chamfer and any vibration / screed tolerance. If the drawing gives the foundation dimension (excavation footprint), do not confuse it with the block dimension.

- Fixed-tilt vs tracker. Tracker foundations have tighter tolerance and often a different bearing-plate layout. The mould for a tracker pier usually needs an ABS insert to hold the bolt positions within ±1 mm. Tell us which mounting system you are using.

- Groove and cable routing. The groove is not decorative — it is where the support leg sits or where DC cables cross. Give the groove width, depth and whether it is open on one end (for cable pass-through) or closed on all four sides.

- Lifting and handling. A 30 × 30 × 30 cm concrete block weighs about 65 kg; larger piers can be 150–400 kg. If the blocks are being machine-placed, we cast in a lifting socket or hole. If they are hand-placed, a finger groove on two sides is enough. Tell us how they will be handled on site.

## Have a solar foundation drawing?
Send the pier section, bolt layout and project quantity. We will come back within one working day with mould feasibility, material choice, lead time and an FOB Ningbo/Shanghai price.

Floating PV shore basesPrecast anchor blocks and shore-side connection piers for floating solar installations on reservoirs and lakes.

## Photovoltaic Pier Moulds — FAQ

## What are the standard PV pier mould sizes?
The two catalogue sizes we keep in tooling are 30 × 20 × 30 cm and 30 × 30 × 30 cm (length × width × height), available as grooved flat piers or plain flat piers. Most utility-scale projects use a custom size from the foundation drawing — those are cut to order.

## Can you cast bolt pockets, anchor plates or cable grooves into the block?
Yes. Send the bolt size (M12 / M16 / M20 are common), centre-to-centre spacing, projection, and whether it is cast-in or post-installed. We build bolt pockets and embed-plate recesses directly into the mould so each block comes out ready to accept the mounting hardware without drilling.

## What is the difference between a fixed-tilt pier and a tracker pier mould?
Tracker piers have tighter positional tolerance on the bearing-plate bolts (typically ±1 mm rather than ±3 mm) and often a different plate size. For tracker work we usually recommend an ABS insert in a PP mould body — the insert holds tolerance over many pours while the PP body keeps the mould affordable.

## Which material should I choose — PP or ABS?
PP is the default for standard grooved / plain piers and gives 150+ pour cycles. ABS is the better choice when the bolt pattern has to hold tight tolerance over thousands of pours (most tracker jobs), or when the mould has fine detail. Piers are simple rectangular shapes, so PP covers nearly all standard projects.

## How much does a 30 × 30 × 30 cm concrete pier weigh?
A solid 30 × 30 × 30 cm block is about 65 kg at standard 2,400 kg/m³ concrete. If your blocks will be placed by hand, add finger grooves to two sides of the mould. For machine placement, ask us to cast in a lifting socket or hole.

## What is the lead time for a custom PV pier mould?
Simple modifications to a catalogue size (e.g. adding a groove or bolt pocket): 10–15 working days. A brand-new profile from a foundation drawing: 20–30 working days. Lead time is confirmed in writing after drawing review and deposit.

## Can I mix different pier sizes in one order?
Yes. Most solar farms use two to four pier sizes across the site. Mixed-size orders can share one 20 ft or 40 HC container; we palletize by size and mark each pallet with the pier dimensions and quantity.

## Do you mould rooftop ballast blocks as well as ground piers?
Yes, but they are different products. Ground piers anchor the racking with cast-in bolts or pockets; rooftop ballast blocks hold the array down by weight without penetrating the waterproof membrane, so they are usually lower and wider and are sized from the roof's allowable load (kg/m²), wind zone and rail section. Send the roof-load and wind data and we mould the size the engineering calls for.

## How many blocks does a solar farm need — blocks per MW?
There is no fixed number per MW: it follows the racking layout, support spacing, wind/snow zone and whether the array is fixed-tilt, ballasted-roof or tracker. Count the support/pier locations from your racking layout drawing, add a small breakage allowance, and confirm block weight against on-site handling (a solid 30×30×30 block is about 65 kg). Send us the layout and we can review the quantity and size list with you.

PV farms also use these alongside pier foundations on the DC-side and civil scope.

## Power Engineering Concrete Mould Buyer Guide

Most of this catalogue is coping (wall cap) moulds for cable trenches and substation boundaries, plus corner pieces, transformer platform copings, cobblestone moulds and ground anchor moulds. Sizes below are the actual mould dimensions we hold, from 28.5 cm short caps up to 110 cm long units.

## What is actually in this category

- Power coping moulds (straight runs): the volume product. Widths 12.5–34 cm, heights 6–25 cm, lengths 28.5, 40, 74.5, 75, 80 and 100 cm. Plain, strip, double-line, double-arc and grooved profiles.

- Coping corner moulds: 47×25×15, 50×25×15, 64–49×20×6 and 80–80×15×12 cm, including a welded-type corner.

- Transformer equipment copings: 90×20×20 and 110×15×10 cm, supplied as A/B left-right pairs.

- Cobblestone combination moulds: 6×10 cm, 10×15 cm and a 10-cavity version for 8 cm spheres, used for decorative revetment and cable-corridor surfacing.

- Other utility parts: boundary wall pillar coping 42×42×8.3 cm, L-shaped cable trench coping 100×25×20 cm, ground anchor mould 56×28×13 cm.

## Three things buyers get wrong on these moulds

- A corner marked “64–49” is not 64 by 49 cm. On corner and curved coping pieces the two numbers are the outer and inner arc length of the same part — 64 cm along the outside face, 49 cm along the inside. If you quote it as a rectangle you will order the wrong mould. Always confirm which face your drawing dimensions follow.

- A cobblestone mould is two pieces, not one. These are A+B combination moulds: the A half and B half close together to form the sphere cavities. A single half is not usable on its own, so quantity must be counted in sets.

- Transformer copings ship as left/right pairs. The 90×20×20 and 110×15×10 cm units are marked A (left) and B (right) because the platform corners mirror each other. Buying one side only will leave the platform unfinished.

## Matching coping to your trench, not to a price list

Coping sits on top of a cable trench wall or boundary wall, so the mould width has to follow your wall thickness — not the other way round. This is why the same 100 cm length appears here in 15, 20, 25 and 34 cm widths.

- Measure the finished wall thickness first, then pick the coping width that overhangs evenly on both faces.

- Decide the top profile before quoting: flat, single arc, double arc, or double-line grooved. It changes the mould, not just the finish.

- For runs with bends, count corner pieces separately and state the corner angle and arc lengths.

- One 100×20×20 cm coping in this catalogue is dimensioned to sit with China Southern Power Grid cover slabs. If your project follows a specific grid standard, say so in the enquiry.

## Material choice: PP or ABS

Several coping moulds here exist in both PP and ABS. ABS holds a sharper edge on grooved and double-arc profiles and tolerates more handling on site; PP is the lower-cost option for plain profiles in high-cycle yard production.

- Choose ABS when the visible top profile has fine grooves or tight arcs.

- Choose PP for plain, flat-topped coping produced in large repeat volumes.

- Either way, typical service life is 150+ pour cycles with normal demoulding practice.

## Power Engineering Moulds FAQ

## How do I read a size like “64–49 × 20 × 6” on a corner coping mould?
The first two numbers are the outer and inner arc length of the same corner piece, not length by width. That part measures 64 cm along its outer face and 49 cm along its inner face, with a 20 cm width and 6 cm height. When you send a drawing, state clearly which face your dimension follows, otherwise the corner will not close against the straight runs.

## Is a cobblestone combination mould one piece or two?
Two. The A half and B half close together to form the sphere cavities, so they are ordered and counted in sets. We hold 6×10 cm and 10×15 cm versions plus a 10-cavity mould for 8 cm spheres.

## Why are the transformer equipment copings sold as pairs?
Because the platform corners mirror each other. The 90×20×20 cm and 110×15×10 cm units are marked A (left) and B (right); ordering only one side leaves the opposite corner without a matching cap.

## How do I choose the coping width?
Start from the finished thickness of the trench or boundary wall the coping sits on, then select a width that overhangs evenly on both faces. That is why the same 100 cm length is held in 15, 20, 25 and 34 cm widths.

## Should I choose PP or ABS for coping moulds?
Choose ABS when the top profile has fine grooves or tight double arcs, since it holds a sharper edge and takes more handling. Choose PP for plain flat-topped coping produced in large repeat volumes. Typical service life is 150+ pour cycles either way.

## Can power engineering moulds ship together with cable trench moulds?
Yes. Coping, corner pieces, trench moulds and cover moulds can be mixed in one shipment where packing allows, which is usually how project orders are consolidated.

## Do you provide fixed public prices for these moulds?
No. These are quoted by size, top profile, material and order quantity, so we issue project quotations rather than a public price list. Send your component schedule with quantities per size for a factory quote.

## Rail Transit Concrete Moulds FAQ

## Which railway standard do the grid emblem covers follow?
The grid-pattern covers carry the China Railway emblem (Tie Biao / railway standard) and are used on railway subgrade drainage and cable trenches. Sizes include 40×32×6.6cm and 65.4×49.4×6.3cm; send your project drawing or standard code so we match the exact emblem, tread and dimensions.

## Are the stepped transition cover variants interchangeable?
No. The 85×13×14.3cm stepped covers come in three step profiles (step 37.5 / 42.5 / 55.5). Each mould produces only one step height, so specify the step profile and the trench height difference rather than ordering by outer size alone.

## What are the fence footing blocks used for?
The 39×22×12cm and 39×22×12.5cm footing blocks are precast foundations for high-speed-rail and railway subgrade fence posts. Formed sockets and a drainage opening let the post locate quickly without cast-in-situ concrete; confirm your post section and embedment depth.

## Can you supply the full bridge/viaduct railing component set?
Yes. The range covers I-beam (72×93.7×5cm) and seagull railing panels, Type-72 integral telescopic expansion posts (for deck expansion joints), slotted connection posts, and standard-section 1295/1175mm and 1695/1575mm handrail/support beams. Components from one system are designed to lock together.

## Which material — PP or ABS — for rail transit moulds?
Thin subgrade covers and fence footings can use PP. Large bridge/viaduct panels and long 1.3–1.7m handrail/beam moulds with deep ribs and tight notches use ABS for stiffness, dimension holding and repeated pours over long project quantities.

## Do you mark a load-bearing class on the cover moulds?
No, and buyers should not request one on a mould. Load capacity is a property of the finished concrete cover (rebar design, concrete grade and slab thickness), not of the plastic mould. We mould the cover dimensions, emblem and tread; structural design follows the project engineering drawing.

## Can these moulds be made from project drawings?
Yes. Rail transit components almost always follow project or local standards. Send the finished component drawing, section profile, application (subgrade trench, fence run, bridge deck) and quantity, and we will confirm catalogue fit or OEM tooling.

## Do you supply project-specific railway step plates (e.g. He-An-Jiu Type A / Type B)?
Yes. Dedicated railway access/step plates — such as the He-An-Jiu (合安九) line Type A and Type B step plates — are made to the project standard drawing rather than as catalogue items; the B-type is a roughly 67×32×8–21cm stepped profile. Send the standard drawing or a marked photo and we confirm the profile, number per kilometre and lead time as custom tooling. These sit alongside the catalogue 85×13×14.3 stepped trench covers (step 37.5/42.5/55.5), which are a different, stocked product.

## Slope Protection Mould Buyer Guide

Slope protection mould selection starts from the finished block face size and the slope gradient, not from the mould price. The 21 sizes on this page span 29–59 cm long, 15–44 cm wide and 5–24 cm thick.

## Block types on this page

- Ecological grass-planting blocks: open-cell blocks that let vegetation root through the slope face. Most common family, 29–50 cm formats.

- River channel blocks: heavy 24 cm-thick sections with 3–4 cm drainage holes for canal and river-bank lining.

- Hydraulic capping blocks: tapered top-of-slope closing pieces (45 × 36.9 × 10 cm, top face 35 cm).

- Companion block sets: smaller infill units laid together with a main block to close out a bonding pattern.

## Three things buyers get wrong

- Thickness is a structural choice, not a cost option. On this page thickness runs 5–24 cm for a similar face size. A thinner block is cheaper per piece but is specified for gentler slopes and lower flow velocity — match it to the design, not to the budget.

- A quoted size like 16.2–15 cm is draft taper, not a tolerance. The block is 16.2 cm at one face and 15 cm at the other so it releases from the mould. Do not read it as "±0.6 cm".

- Grass-planting void ratio drives the vegetation result. Two blocks with the same outer size can differ from roughly 25% to 35% open area. Ask for the void ratio, not just the block dimensions.

ApplicationSuitable block typeKey parameters

River bank & canal liningRiver channel blocks, thick ecological blocksBlock thickness, drainage hole size, flow velocity
Highway / railway embankmentEcological grass-planting blocksFace size, open-void ratio, slope gradient
Top of slope closing courseHydraulic capping blocksTop and bottom face width, taper
Pattern infill & edgesCompanion block setsMain block size it pairs with

## Stepped & I-Shaped Slope Block Mould Buyer Guide

I-shaped (also called dogbone or H-shaped) slope blocks lock into each other along the slope by shape alone, which is why they are specified where a plain rectangular block would slide. This page holds 11 sizes from 26 to 50 cm long.

## I-shaped vs half-I: what actually differs

- Full I-shaped block: waisted on both sides, so it keys into neighbours on all four edges. Used across the main slope field.

- Half-I block: waisted on one side and straight on the other. It is the edge and closing piece — you order it alongside the full block, not instead of it.

- Interlocking I-shaped block: I-profile plus tongue-and-groove edges and open grass-planting voids, for slopes that need both mechanical keying and vegetation.

## Three things buyers get wrong

- Ordering only the full block. Every slope has edges. If you order 100% full I-blocks you will be cutting them on site to close the boundary. Work out the half-I quantity from the slope perimeter at drawing stage.

- Reading the quoted size as the finished paved module. An I-shaped block interlocks, so the laid centre-to-centre spacing is smaller than the block's overall length. Ask for the laying module if you are calculating blocks per m².

- Assuming same face size means interchangeable. This page has 40 × 30 cm blocks at 10, 12 and 15 cm thick, and two 50 × 30 × 10 cm blocks of different profile (I and half-I). Same footprint, different mould, different product.

Position on slopeBlock to useKey parameters

Main slope fieldFull I-shaped blockFace size, thickness, waist width
Slope edges & closing courseHalf-I blockMust match the field block's size and thickness
Slope needing vegetationInterlocking I-shaped block with voidsVoid count and open area
Higher flow / steeper slopeThicker section (15 cm)Thickness per structural design

## Stepping Stone Mould Buyer Guide

Stepping stone mould orders are usually driven by the surface pattern, finished slab size and thickness, plus whether the paving is walked on directly or set into gravel or lawn.

## Typical stepping stone mould types

- Round stepping stones: Ø35–50cm discs for lawn and gravel paths, cast 5–6cm thick.

- Faux stone slabs: irregular stone texture in 5×5cm up to 100×45cm, including 1-out-N multi-cavity moulds.

- Wood-grain walkway stones: 90–200cm long strips imitating timber decking and sleepers.

- Patterned garden tiles: lotus, cloud, fret, coin and blessing motifs for courtyards and temple paving.

## Project drawing checklist

For stepping stone and paving tile moulds, the key parameters are the finished slab dimensions, thickness and surface pattern. A photo of the target paving helps us match the texture.

- Confirm finished slab length × width × thickness.

- Send a photo or sketch of the required surface pattern or texture.

- State whether the units are laid on sand, gravel, lawn or mortar bed.

ApplicationSuitable mould typeKey parameters

Garden / lawn pathRound stepping stones, faux stone slabsDiameter or slab size, thickness, texture
Patio / courtyard pavingPatterned garden tiles, litchi-texture stoneTile size, pattern, thickness, layout repeat
Park & scenic walkwayWood-grain walkway and strip stonesStrip length, width, thickness, grain direction

## Stepping Stone Mould FAQ

## Striped Drainage Cover Mould Buyer Guide

How to specify striped concrete drain covers for pedestrian and landscape drainage before requesting a quotation.

## Where striped covers are used

- Pedestrian and park drainage: the raised stripe pattern gives a directional walking surface on covers that sit flush with paving.

- Plaza and streetscape trench runs: long covers laid end to end read as a continuous linear feature rather than separate lids.

- Notched variants: a notch on one or both ends lets the cover seat into a channel shoulder instead of resting on top.

- Common sizes in this range: 44.4×49.4×6cm, 49.4×44.4×6cm, 59×50×10cm, 73×49×10cm and 79.4×49.4×6cm.

## Specification notes

Striped covers are cast face-down, so the stripe geometry sits in the base of the mould. Deeper, narrower stripes look sharper but need more vibration to fill and more draft to release cleanly. Send the channel opening size first — the cover has to match the channel, not the other way round.

- Give the finished concrete size, not the mould outside size.

- State whether the cover needs an end notch and on how many sides.

- Say if you cast with a steel identification plate — the pattern layout has to leave room for it.

Buyer needRecommended mould directionQuote details to prepare

Park or sidewalk trench coverStriped cover mould, 6cm thickness classChannel clear opening, cover length × width, stripe direction
Cover that seats into the channelNotched striped cover mouldNotch size and which ends are notched, seat depth
Heavier plaza or light-vehicle areaStriped cover mould, 8-10cm thickness classExpected load, reinforcement plan, finished thickness

## How the Anti-Slip Ribbed Face Is Formed

A ribbed anti-slip cover mould turned over so you can see the full cavity. The grooves are cast in the same pour as the slab — nothing is cut or treated afterwards. Groove depth, direction and draft angle decide whether the cover demoulds cleanly and still grips underfoot. Tell us your cover size and we will match a ribbed pattern to it.

## FAQ

## Are striped drainage cover moulds only decorative?
No. They are functional concrete drainage covers with a striped surface pattern. The pattern improves appearance and can add slip resistance.

## Can you customize the cover size and hole pattern?
Yes. Send the cover size, load requirement, hole or slot drawing and sample photo for review.

## Which buyers need this mould type?
Precast factories, landscape contractors, municipal suppliers and drainage channel buyers looking for a finished cover surface.

## Traditional Chinese Architecture Mould Buyer Guide

Roof ridges, ridge-end ornaments, Paofang wall bands, gable bargeboards, wall coping and decorative blocks — match the mould to where the part sits on the building and the regional style.

## Four mould groups on this page

- Roof ridges: sugarcane/imitation-tile/ruyi/round-bead/drum ridge beams 50–62cm, all in rigid PP/ABS — one mould per ridge profile.

- Ridge-end & blocks: Bogu ridge heads (57×31×19) and small 'Wen Dou' ornamental blocks ~20cm with Wan lattice or Fu character, cap-and-base sets.

- Paofang wall bands: horizontal wall/eave trim 50–80cm long; PP & ABS; one-piece or left/mid/right combo; L-shaped and cover pieces.

- Bargeboard, coping & ornaments: gable bargeboard combo sets, three-line/tile-bed wall coping for 18/24-brick walls, ruyi plaques, floral panels and meander/fret blocks.

## Three things buyers get wrong

- Mixing up ridge, wall band and bargeboard. They look similar in photos but go on the roof top, the wall face and the gable slope respectively — specify by location.

- Ordering combo sets by the middle piece only. Bargeboards and Paofang sets need left + right end pieces plus the repeating middle section; ends are handed and cannot be swapped.

- Treating thin bands as structural. Paofang/bargeboard pieces are 3–10cm facade trim with a demoulding taper ('3-2cm'); use three-line coping for load-bearing wall caps.

Project needRecommended mould directionQuote details to prepare

Chinese-style roof (temple, hall, gateway)Roof ridge beam + ridge-end ornament (one mould per profile)Roof slope/length, ridge style (Suzhou/Huizhou), reference photo

Courtyard wall top trimPaofang wall band combo set (left/mid/right) + cover piecesWall run length, band height/thickness, pattern, PP or ABS

Gable edge finishingGable bargeboard combo set (left/middle/right)Gable rake length and slope, number of middle sections

Load-bearing wall capThree-line / tile-bed wall coping (18- or 24-brick)Wall thickness (18/24 brick), coping width, tile support yes/no

Wall face decorationRuyi plaques, floral panels, meander/fret blocksPattern, block size, spacing, smooth or textured face

## Traditional Chinese Architecture Mould FAQ

## What kinds of traditional Chinese architecture moulds are on this page?
Five families: (1) compound wall coping caps and antique-style integrated wall tiles (围墙压顶/仿古连体瓦) — load-bearing coping caps in 40–60cm sections with matching corners and inner forms, plus Type-37/Type-50 one-piece tiled wall crowns; (2) roof ridge moulds — the horizontal ridge beams that cap a Chinese-style roof, including the smooth round 'sugarcane' ridge (甘蔗脊), imitation-tile ridge (假瓦脊), ruyi-pattern ridge (如意脊), round-bead ridge (圆珠脊) and cylindrical drum ridge (滚筒脊),; (3) ridge-end ornaments & decorative blocks — Bogu antique ridge heads (万字博古), ridge-end cap blocks, and small 'Wen Dou' ornamental blocks with Wan lattice (万字文斗) or Fu character (福字文斗), with cap-and-base sets; (4) Paofang (抛枋) decorative wall bands / eave mouldings — the horizontal trim strips that run along the top of courtyard walls, in PP and ABS, one-piece (连体) or left/middle/right combo sets, L-shaped and with cover pieces; and (5) gable bargeboard sets (博风板), three-line / tile-bed wall coping (三线板/瓦托底) for 18- and 24-brick walls, and wall ornaments — ruyi appliqué plaques (如意贴), wall-hung floral panels (挂墙花板) and meander/fret pattern blocks (回文正古).

## Who uses these moulds outside China — can they be made for overseas projects?
Yes. These moulds serve Chinese-style temples, clan halls, courtyard restaurants and teahouses, Chinatown gateways, Chinese gardens and landscape walls, and luxury residential projects that want a Suzhou (苏派) or Huizhou/Anhui (徽派 — white walls, dark tile) look in South-east Asia, North America and beyond. We name each part in plain English by its function (roof ridge, wall band, bargeboard, coping, ornament block) so the drawing is unambiguous. Send reference photos or CAD; we confirm the regional style and quote the matching mould set.

## What is the difference between a roof ridge, a Paofang wall band and a bargeboard?
They sit in three different places and are the most commonly confused parts. The roof ridge (屋脊) runs along the very top of the tiled roof and is often curved or round. The Paofang wall band (抛枋/抛方线条) is a flat decorative trim strip mounted horizontally on the upper wall or eave line — typically 50–80cm long and only 3.5–10cm thick, sometimes in left/middle/right sections. The bargeboard (博风板) is the sloped board that trims the gable end (rake) of a roof, and also comes as left/middle/right combo pieces. Ordering by location — roof top, wall face, or gable slope — avoids mixing them up.

## How do the left / middle / right combo-set moulds work?
Both bargeboards (博风板) and some Paofang bands are supplied as a set of three moulds: left end piece (左端/左边板), straight middle section (中段/中间段) and right end piece (右端/右边板). The middle section repeats along the run; the two end pieces finish the corners and are handed — a left end cannot be used as a right end. Order the full set (one left + one right + however many middle sections per metre of run), not just the middle, or the corners will not close out.

## What do thickness figures like '3-2cm' or '6.5 / 3 / 2' mean on the thin bands and covers?
These thin decorative pieces are drafted (tapered) for demoulding, so the wall is thicker at one face and thinner at the other — '3-2' means 3cm tapering to 2cm, and 'thickness 3 / 2' marks the same taper on the cover. It is a designed draft angle, not a tolerance. Paofang bands, bargeboards and their covers are facade trim, not load-bearing elements; do not specify them as structural coping. Load-bearing wall caps use the three-line / tile-bed coping (三线板) instead.

## Should these moulds be PP or ABS?
All Zhihua moulds are injection-moulded rigid plastic — PP or ABS; we do not make silicone, PU or rubber moulds. Standard blocks and ridges cast well in PP for 150+ pours. ABS is used for the long thin Paofang bands (e.g. 80×22×5, 60×8×6) and L-shaped/cover pieces, where a stiffer wall keeps the thin edge and fine line pattern straight over hundreds of casts. We recommend PP or ABS per piece based on size, pattern depth and your volume.

## What is the MOQ, lead time and can patterns be customised?
Mixed-SKU orders are welcome with no strict MOQ on catalogue pieces. Custom regional styles, new patterns (ruyi, meander/fret, Wan lattice, Fu character) and combo sets are made to order, typically 15–30 days after drawing approval. These moulds are light and nest well for container loading; send drawings, quantities, style reference and destination port for an FOB Ningbo/Shanghai quote.

## Tree Ring Mould Buyer Guide

Tree ring mould selection starts from the finished tree pit diameter, then works back to whether a one-piece ring, a modular set or straight-and-corner segments is most economical.

## Typical tree ring mould types

- Modular multi-piece sets: four-piece and eight-piece kits that combine into different pit diameters from one mould family.

- Decorative round rings: sunburst, cast-iron-look, cloud and petal motifs in 50×50 to 64.5×64.5cm formats.

- Straight, elbow & corner segments: 40–150cm segments for square, rectangular and free-form pit surrounds.

- Planter & garden edging stones: 40×27×6cm and 73×9×14cm units for planting bed and lawn borders.

## Project drawing checklist

For tree ring moulds, the finished tree pit opening and the surround width drive everything else. Tell us the pit size and we can advise which segment combination is cheapest.

- State the finished tree pit opening (inner diameter or clear square).

- Confirm surround width, height and whether a corner piece is needed.

- Say whether the ring is flush with paving or raised as a kerb.

## Tree Ring Mould FAQ

## What is a concrete tree ring used for?
Concrete tree rings surround street and park trees to protect the root zone, keep soil in place, stop pedestrians compacting the pit and give the streetscape a finished edge. They are also called tree grates or tree pit surrounds.

## How do modular tree ring sets work?
A modular set uses repeated straight units plus corner units. By changing how many straight units are used per side, one mould kit can build several tree pit sizes, which lowers mould cost on multi-size projects.

## Can you supply moulds for a specific tree pit diameter?
Yes. Tell us the finished pit opening and surround width. We can recommend a catalogue combination or quote an OEM mould for the exact profile.

# Guide: Cable Trench Cover Moulds Buying Guide: Lift-Handle Power, Metro & Tunnel Covers
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/cable-trench-moulds-buying-guide

Buying Guide

## Cable Trench Cover Moulds Buying Guide: Lift-Handle Power, Metro & Tunnel Covers
How to choose precast concrete cable trench cover moulds — removable lift-handle power/utility covers, metro/subway and deep-burial tunnel trough covers; sizes, seat/notch detail, PP vs ABS and OEM quote checklist.

Published June 14, 2026 · Updated September 8, 2026 · Zhihua Moulds

## What a cable trench cover actually is

A cable trench is the shallow concrete or brick-lined channel that runs alongside substations, industrial parks, railway platforms and tunnel walls to carry power and telecom cables. The part most buyers actually need to precast in volume — and the part this guide covers — is the removable concrete cover slab that seats on top of that trench. It has to protect the cables, carry foot or light vehicle traffic, and still lift out when a crew needs to pull new cable or inspect the run.

That last requirement drives the design. Unlike a fixed drainage slab, a cable trench cover is opened repeatedly, often for decades. So the mould is built around lift points — moulded lifting slots (a common size is 8.5×3.5cm), recessed handles, or through-holes for a hook — plus a seat that locates the slab on the trench wall without rocking.

## The four cover families we mould

- Lift-handle power / utility covers. The workhorse for substations and utility corridors. Rectangular slabs from roughly 60×40cm up to 170×50cm, with moulded lifting slots or pull points. Typical specs include 80×50×6, 74×40×8, 72.5×50.5×5.5 and the wide 170×50×8 power cover.

- Notched and treaded covers. Notched variants (e.g. 71×49×8, 79×50×6 with a 20×1cm notch, 89×49×8) have a moulded side notch for frame or pipe clearance. Cobblestone-tread covers (e.g. 138×40×5) and Tie-Biao striped covers (70×43×6) add anti-slip surface for walk-overs and rail-side trenches.

- Metro / subway covers. Large smooth ABS panels such as the 149×55×5 metro cover, plus multi-part T-junction assembly sets (e.g. 60.8×59×34.4cm) supplied with a demoulding diagram, used where trough runs branch on a platform or underpass.

- Deep-burial tunnel covers. Extra-thick 20–26cm slabs for railway and road tunnel troughs — 60×50×26, 80×50×23 and the 85×49×20 type-B section — engineered to tunnel drawings.

You can see all of these with dimensions on the cable trench cover moulds product page.

## How to size a cover from your trench (the most common mistake)

Buyers frequently send the trench inner width and assume that is the cover width. It is not. The cover has to overhang the wall to form a bearing seat on each side. A 170×50cm cover typically seats over a much narrower trench opening — the extra width is the two seat bearings plus any frame. To size correctly, send:

- the trench clear opening (inner width × inner depth);

- the wall/seat width at the top, so the cover bearing length is known;

- the required cover thickness (driven by your load environment, not by us);

- whether slabs should be single-span across the opening or split.

Get the seat wrong and the slab either rocks (too narrow, no bearing) or won't drop in (too wide, binds on the frame).

## Notches, lifting slots and treads — moulded, never cut

A frame-clearance notch, a drainage slot or a lifting hole must be formed by the mould, not ground or cut on site. Cutting a notch into a cured slab cuts the rebar cover and creates a crack initiation point right where load concentrates. The same applies to anti-slip treads: cobblestone and striped patterns are moulded into the top face so the slip resistance is integral, not a coating that wears off. If your cover needs an orientation mark (so crews don't seat it upside down), we can mould an UP arrow into the face.

## PP vs ABS: which to specify

Polypropylene (PP) is the default and lower-cost choice. It flexes slightly, demoulds cleanly and is ideal for standard lift covers up to about 80cm in high-cycle yard production. ABS is stiffer and more rigid — specify it for large panels (100–170cm), the 20–26cm deep tunnel sections, and metro T-junction assembly sets, where the mould has to hold a precise multi-part geometry through hundreds of pours. As a rule of thumb: everyday removable cover in PP; big, deep or assembled section in ABS.

## About load ratings — read this before you ask for one

We mould the concrete form; we do not stamp a load class onto it. Whether a cover carries foot traffic, a pickup or a service truck depends on the finished reinforced concrete — the rebar design, concrete grade and slab thickness — not on the plastic mould. We provide the geometry, wall/rib layout and thickness your drawing calls for; the structural rating is certified by the precaster's concrete design. If a project spec cites a load class, send that and we confirm the mould can produce the required section.

## What to send for a fast, accurate quote

- Cover length × width × thickness, plus the trench clear opening and seat width.

- Type: lift-handle removable, notched, cobblestone/striped tread, metro panel or deep-burial tunnel slab.

- Lifting-slot or handle positions, any notch or drainage slots, and any orientation marking.

- Application: substation/power, telecom, industrial park, metro/subway, or railway/road tunnel — this drives our PP/ABS recommendation.

- Material preference, quantity by size, destination port, and whether mixed sizes ship together.

For OEM sections, a dimensioned drawing is best; clear photos from several angles work for a feasibility check. Trench body (U-channel) moulds are a separate range — see the drainage channel / U-channel moulds page.

## Frequently asked questions

## Do you sell the trench body or just the cover moulds?
This range is the cover programme — removable lift-handle and metro/tunnel covers. U-shaped trench body moulds are a separate, section-quoted range; tell us if you need both and we will quote the body from your section drawing.

## Why do cable trench covers have lifting slots?
Cable trenches are opened repeatedly for cable pulling and inspection. Moulded slots or handles (commonly 8.5×3.5cm) let a crew lift the slab with a hook or bar and seat it flush again, with no cast-iron frame to rust or seize.

## What cover size fits my trench opening?
The cover is wider than the clear opening because it overhangs to form a bearing seat on each wall. Send the inner opening, the wall/seat width and the required thickness — for example a 170×50 cover suits a narrower opening — and we match the mould.

## Can the cover have a notch or anti-slip pattern?
Yes. Notches, drainage slots, lifting holes and cobblestone or Tie-Biao striped treads are all moulded in. They must be moulded rather than cut on site, since cutting a cured slab damages the rebar cover and starts cracks.

## Should I choose PP or ABS?
PP for standard lift covers up to around 80cm and high-volume yard production; ABS for large 100–170cm panels, 20–26cm deep tunnel sections and metro T-junction assembly sets that need a stiffer, dimensionally stable mould.

## Can you certify a load rating?
Load class is a property of the finished reinforced concrete (rebar, concrete grade, thickness), not of the plastic mould. We produce the section your drawing and load spec require; the structural rating is certified by the precaster's concrete design.

# Guide: Colored, Decorative & Grass Paver Moulds Buying Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/colored-decorative-grass-paver-moulds-buying-guide

“Colored paver moulds” (彩色路面砖 / cai zhuan) cover a surprisingly wide family: everything from hollow units that grow grass, through municipal accessibility tiles, to decorative tiles embossed with flowers and leaves. Buyers run into trouble when they treat them as one product. This guide separates the families and lists the points that actually decide whether a paving job succeeds.

## 1. The five paver families in this range

- Permeable / grass-grid pavers. Hollow units with through planting holes. Our range has hexagonal units (outer 12.5 and 13.5 cm, inner holes 5 and 5.5 cm) and a large 48 × 24 × 8 cm serrated slab with two circular through holes. Holes are filled with soil and seed (or gravel) after laying.

- Tactile pavers. Accessibility tiles for visually impaired pedestrians: blister (raised dot) warning tiles and strip (directional) tiles, in 20 × 20 × 6 cm and 25 × 25 × 5 cm, normally bright yellow.

- Shaped / interlocking pavers. Diamond, bow, arrow, clover, crescent, tooth and serrated shapes that interlock or build landscape patterns, plus combination sets.

- Square & interlocking workhorses. 18–30 cm square colored pavers (including 2–3 cm thin overlays), I/H-shaped interlockers and anti-slip grid-face tiles — the volume sellers for sidewalks and community roads.

- Patterned decorative tiles. Embossed faces — maple leaf, plum blossom, chrysanthemum, diamond, Spanish, nine-grid and double-fan — plus small 12.5 cm hexagons, for courtyards, parks and scenic paving.

## 2. Solid vs hollow — the first question to answer

Most “colored pavers” are solid tiles that simply pave. Only the permeable hexagons and the holed 48 cm slab in this range are hollow: their through holes exist to drain stormwater and grow grass (sponge-city / green-parking applications). A common mistake is buying shaped decorative tiles that look lacy and assuming they will drain — clover and crescent shapes are solid; check for actual through holes before specifying a permeable pavement.

## 3. Grass-grid pavers fail on sub-base, not on the tile

A hollow grass paver carries light vehicle loads only when the system is built correctly: open-graded crushed-stone sub-base (free-draining), compacted and level, geotextile separation where specified, holes filled with a soil/gravel mix suited to the seed. Poured onto a flat sand bed with no drainage, the grass dies in weeks and the slab cracks under tyres. The mould is the easy part — the base design is what buyers forget.

## 4. Thickness means duty

- 2–3 cm: overlay/veneer tiles bonded onto sound existing pavement — not structural.

- 4–5 cm: foot traffic — sidewalks, plazas, courtyards.

- 6 cm: community roads and light vehicle areas, especially interlocking shapes.

- 8 cm: occasional vehicle loads (serrated/drainage slabs, thick interlockers).

Interlocking I/H and tooth shapes outperform plain squares on vehicles because the joints transfer load across the pavement — that is why driveway specifications call for interlockers, not large plain slabs.

## 5. Patterns are laid, not just cast

Four-piece motifs (plum blossom, chrysanthemum) need four tiles per complete flower: order in multiples of four, and decide the laying direction before work starts. Continuous patterns (Spanish, double-fan) likewise need a direction plan and consistent pouring orientation. Sort this out at the layout stage — rotating a quarter-tile after the concrete has set means cutting out finished pavers.

## 6. Color is made in the mix

Colored pavers get their color from iron-oxide pigment mixed into the concrete (typically 2–5% of cement weight by color depth). For thick tiles a pigmented wear-course layer poured first, then plain base concrete, gives the same surface color at lower pigment cost. White cement is used for bright pastels; grey cement for deep reds, yellows and greens. PP and ABS mould faces don't react with oxide pigments and release cleanly, so the color stays even tile to tile.

## 7. Tactile tiles are a compliance item, not decoration

Blister dots = stop/hazard/turn warning; long strips = safe directional line. Municipal sidewalks, stations, hospitals and public buildings require them, usually in attention-grabbing yellow. If a project includes public-access paving, the tactile tiles should be in the same mould order as the running pavers so heights and batch color match.

## 8. Cavities, materials and output

“1-out-N” is the number of tiles per pour — a 1-out-9 mould makes nine rough-stone tiles in one cycle, cutting cost and labour per tile on volume runs. PP is the default (150+ cycles, flexible demoulding); ABS is chosen for deep crisp motifs and fine textures that must stay sharp. Compare quotes per finished tile and per daily output, not per mould.

## Build a balanced first order

If you are importing paver block moulds for the first time, a mixed-SKU order is usually safer than committing to one pattern. A practical mix pairs a few high-volume workhorses — 25–30 cm square/interlocking colored pavers and I/H-shaped interlockers for sidewalks — with a smaller set of decorative shapes (maple leaf, crescent, four-piece flower motifs) and one or two permeable grass-grid or tactile items to win municipal and parking jobs. This lets you test which shapes your local market actually buys before reordering in volume; mixed-SKU packing is standard and there is no strict MOQ per design.

## What to send for a fast quote

- A layout sketch or photo of the paving effect you want

- Tile size and thickness (outer/inner for hollow units)

- Application: footway, driveway, parking, fire lane, plaza or tactile path

- Solid or hollow (grass/permeable)

- Pattern and motif counts (remember multiples of four for flower sets)

- Cavities wanted (1-out-N), PP or ABS, quantities and destination port

Browse the full range on our concrete paver block moulds page — colored, decorative and grass pavers — alongside hexagonal paver moulds and garden stepping stone moulds.

## Planning a colored or grass-paver project?

Send a layout sketch or a photo of the paving effect. We will match standard designs or quote custom patterns and logos.

Request a Quote
