## Frequently Asked Questions

## What is the difference between a colored paver and a grass/permeable paver?
A colored paver (cai zhuan) is a solid decorative or interlocking concrete tile. A grass/permeable paver is hollow, with through holes that are filled with soil and grass (or gravel) after laying, so the surface stays green while carrying light traffic. They are used for parking bays, fire access lanes and sponge-city drainage projects. In our range the hexagonal units (outer 12.5/13.5 cm with 5/5.5 cm inner holes) and the 48x24x8 cm serrated slab with two through holes are hollow; the shaped and patterned pavers are solid.

## How is the color in colored concrete pavers made?
Iron-oxide pigment is mixed into the concrete before pouring, or a thin pigmented wear-course layer is poured first and the base concrete added after (this saves pigment on thick tiles). White cement gives brighter pastel tones; grey cement with pigment gives deeper reds, yellows and greens. Smooth PP/ABS faces release cleanly so color stays even. Pigment dose is typically 2-5% of cement weight by color depth.

## How do I read dimensions like 25 x 25 x 5 cm or outer 12.5 / inner 5 cm?
Solid pavers: length x width x thickness in centimetres. Hollow hexagons: the outer number is the hexagon overall size (opposite-flat distance) and the inner number is the planting/drainage hole. Thin 2-3 cm units are overlay/veneer pavers for resurfacing sound old pavement, not structural slabs for vehicle loads.

## Which pavers can carry cars, and which are only for foot traffic?
Driveways and fire lanes: hollow grass-grid units on an open-graded compacted sub-base, or thick (6-8 cm) interlocking I/H-shaped and tooth/serrated pavers whose joints transfer load. Footways, plazas and courtyards: the decorative shaped and patterned pavers (clover, crescent, bow, diamond, maple leaf, flower motifs). Rule of thumb on thickness: 4-5 cm foot traffic, 6 cm community roads, 8 cm occasional vehicles. Never pave a driveway with 2-3 cm veneer tiles.

## How do four-piece flower patterns work when ordering?
Patterns like plum blossom and chrysanthemum are quartered: each tile carries one quarter of the motif and four tiles laid together form one complete flower. Order in multiples of four tiles per full motif, fix the laying direction before paving starts, and pour consistently so the pattern direction matches. Spanish-style and double-fan patterns are continuous and likewise need a direction plan.

## What are tactile pavers and when are they required?
Tactile (blister/strip) pavers guide visually impaired pedestrians: raised dots (blister/warning tiles) mark hazards, bus stops and turns; long strips (directional tiles) mark the safe walking line. They are mandatory on municipal sidewalks, stations, hospitals and public buildings, usually in bright yellow. We supply both types in 20x20x6 cm and 25x25x5 cm in PP.

## What does 1-out-2 or 1-out-9 mean, and why does it matter for price?
It is the number of finished tiles one mould casts per pour. A 1-out-9 rough-stone mould makes nine 10x10 cm tiles in one cycle. More cavities mean a larger mould but much lower cost and labour per tile. Compare quotes per finished tile and per daily output, not per mould.

## Should paver moulds be PP or ABS?
PP (polypropylene) is the default for high-volume plain and interlocking pavers - it flexes under vibration and demoulding and reaches 150+ pour cycles. ABS is chosen where deep crisp patterns, sharp arrises or fine textures (rough-stone faces, fine anti-slip grooves, deep flower motifs) must stay sharp over hundreds of cycles. Send the pattern and expected volume and we will recommend the grade.

# Guide: Injection Moulding for Rebar Spacers: Concrete Spacer Mould Buying Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/concrete-spacer-block-moulds-buying-guide

Buyers searching for injection moulding for rebar spacer, a rebar spacer mould, a concrete spacer mould (or the US spelling concrete spacer molds) are almost always looking for the same thing: a precision, repeat-use plastic tool that produces the small concrete, mortar or plastic elements holding rebar at the specified cover distance from formwork. These moulds are used in slabs, beams, columns, walls, foundations and precast elements worldwide.

The industry-standard way to make these tools is injection moulding: molten reinforced polypropylene (PP) or ABS is forced under high pressure into a machined steel cavity, producing a one-piece, void-free mould with exact cover-thickness tolerance and smooth walls for clean demoulding. A correctly built injection-moulded rebar spacer mould is typically rated for 150+ concrete pour cycles.

Zhihua runs its own tool shop and injection moulding floor, and supplies injection-moulded concrete spacer block moulds, rebar cover moulds, saddle spacers, bar strip spacers, plum-blossom covers, round disc covers, slot inserts, concrete test specimen moulds and ballast block moulds for both standard catalogue items and OEM profiles from drawings or sample photos.

## 1. Why injection moulding dominates rebar spacer production

There are four reasons the global construction industry settled on injection moulding for rebar spacers rather than thermoforming, 3D printing or welded fabrication:

- Dimensional accuracy. The steel cavity defines cover thickness to a fraction of a millimetre, which matters because code compliance is checked against the finished concrete cover, not the mould nominal size.

- Multi-cavity (1-out-N) output. A single tool can carry 16, 25, 36, 42 or even 100 cavities, so one pour produces many spacers — this is the main lever on piece-cost.

- Cycle life. Reinforced PP/ABS tools survive 150+ concrete pours under normal use without measurable wall wear; thermoformed or printed tools typically fail much earlier.

- One-piece geometry. Saddle clips, plum-blossom centre holes and round-disc rebar seats all need undercuts and ribs that are only economical as a single injection-moulded part.

If a supplier quotes a rebar spacer mould without specifying the plastic material or offering 1-out-N options, they are likely reselling rather than injecting — ask which tonnage press the mould runs on, and whether the steel tool is cut in-house.

## 2. Confirm the application type first

Different markets call similar products by different names: spacer block, rebar cover, saddle spacer, bar strip, plum-blossom cover, round disc cover or concrete chair. Before asking for a quote, decide which structural element the spacer will support.

- Spacer block moulds (square / conical / sloped / U-shaped): used for general cover, foundation work and precast concrete elements.

- Saddle spacers: used in slab-on-grade, raft foundations and mesh support to keep rebar at the right height.

- Bar strip spacers: long, narrow supports for rebar runs in narrow sections or strip footings.

- Plum-blossom rebar covers: round covers with a notched centre for vertical rebar in columns, walls and beams.

- Round disc covers: round covers for vertical rebar in columns, walls and pile caps.

- Slot insert spacers: for rebar with specific cross-section or pipe-insert requirements.

## 3. Specify cover thickness and finished dimensions

For spacer block moulds, the key parameters are the concrete cover thickness, the finished spacer dimensions and the 1-out-N count of the mould. Cover thickness is usually driven by local structural codes (for example 20mm, 25mm, 30mm, 50mm or higher for marine or foundation work).

If only a sample is available, provide clear photos from the front, side and top. Adding a ruler or known-size reference helps the factory judge the dimensions more accurately.

## 4. Choose 1-out-N count that fits your production

Many Zhihua spacer moulds are available in 1-out-N variants such as 1-out-1, 1-out-8, 1-out-16, 1-out-25 or 1-out-100. A higher 1-out-N count speeds up casting for high-volume orders but increases mould size and weight. For distributors and project orders, 1-out-1 or 1-out-16 is usually a good balance between output and handling.

## 5. Match the plastic material to the profile

Two materials dominate injection-moulded rebar spacer moulds:

- Reinforced polypropylene (PP): the default for spacer blocks, saddles, bar strips and most plum-blossom covers. It flexes slightly on demoulding, withstands concrete alkalinity across 150+ cycles, and is the lower-cost option at 1-out-N volumes.

- ABS: chosen for thin-wall, high-precision profiles such as small round-disc spacers and slot inserts where a stiffer, harder wall is needed to hold a tight rebar-seat tolerance.

A reputable injection moulder specifies the material per profile rather than using one generic plastic for every SKU. If you are OEM-ing a custom rebar spacer mould, ask which material is recommended and why — the answer tells you whether the factory understands the application.

## 6. Match spacers to concrete type and finish

Spacer moulds are usually used to cast concrete spacers, but the same mould geometry can also be used for mortar or plastic-aggregate spacers. For visible concrete (architectural finish), choose a spacer type that leaves the smallest possible shadow line.

- Saddle spacers: small shadow, easy to cover with concrete.

- Plum-blossom covers: round shape with a small footprint on column/wall rebar.

- Round disc covers: similar to plum-blossom but with a flat top and simpler geometry.

- Bar strip spacers: ideal for strip footings and narrow sections.

## 7. Include concrete test specimens in the same project

Most rebar projects also require concrete test specimens for cube, cylinder or tensile strength tests. The concrete spacer block moulds catalogue from Zhihua includes 33×6×1.3cm tensile test specimen moulds, 19×4×1.5cm compression specimen moulds, U-shaped no-fines moulds and triangular no-fines block moulds. Combining spacer moulds and test specimen moulds in one shipment is common.

## 8. Pair with ballast block moulds for solar / pile cap work

For solar farms, pile cap foundations or large foundation blocks, ballast block moulds are often ordered together with standard spacer moulds. The current Zhihua catalogue includes Ø36×11cm 22kg round ballast block moulds that pair well with rebar cover spacers in foundation and renewable-energy projects.

## 9. Injection moulding vs other ways of making spacers

Buyers sometimes ask why a rebar spacer mould is quoted as an injection tool when the finished spacers are sold cheaply by the thousand. The distinction matters:

- The finished spacer is a small concrete, mortar or plastic element consumed on site by the thousand.

- The mould is a precision, repeat-use injection-moulded PP/ABS tool that produces those spacers for 150+ pour cycles.

Injection moulding is the only practical process for profiles with rebar-seat undercuts, demoulding ribs and wall thicknesses below 2mm. Compression forming cannot fill these features consistently, and 3D-printed or thermoformed tools wear out long before a production run is complete. That is why every high-volume spacer factory — and every injection moulding for rebar spacer enquiry — ends up at the same process.

## 10. Tool steel, wall thickness and tolerance

The plastic part is only as accurate as the machined steel cavity behind it. Points worth asking about:

- Cavity steel. Production multi-cavity tools are cut from mould steel and polished; a polished wall is what lets green concrete release without tearing the spacer edge.

- Cover tolerance. The finished spacer height should hold within roughly ±0.5mm on small profiles, because code cover is measured on the finished member and a spacer that is 2mm over across a thousand placements accumulates into rework.

- Draft (demoulding taper). Side walls are not parallel: a taper of around 1 degree, sometimes written as 6–5cm on a 100mm-deep part, is intentional, not a tolerance error. It lets the spacer release cleanly.

- Gating and ejector marks. A small gate scar or circular ejector mark on the spacer face is a normal injection-moulding feature, not damage; the current catalogue notes this for large cover plates as well.

## 11. 1-out-N economics: cost per spacer, not cost per mould

The cheapest quote is not the cheapest production. A 1-out-100 tool costs several times a 1-out-8 tool, but the cost per cast spacer can be a fraction once the press time, labour and handling per pour are spread across 100 pieces. The decision tree is simple:

- Trader / distributor / mixed projects: 1-out-1 to 1-out-16 keeps the tool light, the up-front spend low and the mould usable on a small press.

- Dedicated spacer manufacturer: 1-out-25 to 1-out-100 on the highest-running profile (commonly 20/25/30mm saddle or block spacers), with small-cavity tools for the slow sizes.

- Press constraint: check the tool's physical size and required clamping tonnage against your injection machine before buying cavities you cannot cycle.

## 12. From sample to production: the OEM timeline

For non-catalogue profiles, the normal sequence is: photos or drawing with cover thickness and finished dimensions → feasibility and structure review (undercuts, cavity layout, side actions) → quotation → drawing confirmation → steel work and first samples, typically 2–4 weeks for spacer-sized tools → mass production of the mould → shipment. Sending a physical sample by courier gives the fastest and most accurate result; clear front/side/top photos with a ruler are the minimum that works.

## 13. Frequently asked questions

## Is rebar spacer production injection moulding or compression moulding?
Small, precise, thin-wall spacer profiles with undercuts (saddle clips, plum-blossom centre seats, disc rebar seats) are made by injection moulding, because the molten PP/ABS must fill fine ribs and seat geometry under pressure. Simple flat blocks are sometimes vibrated or compression-cast as finished concrete parts, but the reusable moulds themselves are injection-moulded parts. If a supplier cannot tell you which process and press tonnage their moulds run on, they are reselling rather than manufacturing.

## How do I choose the 1-out-N cavity count?
Match cavities to your daily spacer volume and crew. 1-out-1 suits samples, OEM trials and small distributors; 1-out-8 or 1-out-16 is the usual balance for project orders; 1-out-25 to 1-out-100 is for high-volume manufacturers casting thousands of spacers per day. More cavities lower piece cost but make the tool larger, heavier and more expensive up front, and a large multi-cavity tool needs a higher-tonnage injection press. Do not pay for 100 cavities if your press cannot open the tool.

## How long does an OEM spacer mould take, and what does it cost depend on?
A standard catalogue spacer mould is usually in stock. A new OEM profile from a drawing or sample typically takes 2-4 weeks after the drawing is confirmed, depending on cavity count and steel work. Price is driven mainly by cavity count, profile complexity (undercuts and side actions), and material (PP vs ABS), not by the cover-thickness number alone. Sample photos with a ruler are enough to start; a CAD or PDF drawing gives an exact price.

## PP or ABS for a rebar spacer mould?
Reinforced PP is the default: it flexes slightly on demoulding, tolerates concrete alkalinity and reaches 150+ pours at lower cost. ABS is chosen for thin-wall, tight-tolerance profiles such as small round discs and slot inserts, where a stiffer wall keeps the rebar-seat dimension exact. The correct answer is profile-specific; a factory that recommends one plastic for every SKU is not engineering the tool.

## Does the mould carry a warranty or pour-cycle guarantee?
Zhihua rates correctly used PP/ABS injection spacer moulds for 150+ concrete pour cycles with normal release-agent use and careful demoulding. Cycle life is not a property of the plastic alone: aggressive vibration, dry demoulding, steel tools for prying and prolonged UV storage shorten it. More on this in our 150-cycle and demoulding guides linked below.

## Why did my spacer come out with the wrong concrete cover?
Cover is checked on the finished concrete, so the mould must produce the spacer at the exact cover height, including any footing into soft sub-base. On grade, saddle spacers can sink when rebar is placed; use a wider base or a block-type spacer on soft ground. Also confirm whether your drawing gives cover to the rebar centre or to the rebar surface - the two are not interchangeable.

## Can one mould produce several cover thicknesses?
No. Cover height is fixed by the cavity; a 25mm cover mould cannot make 30mm spacers. One mould per profile and cover thickness. If a project uses several covers (slab 25mm, column 40mm, foundation 75mm), order the matching set together - mixed profiles pack in the same shipment and share tooling and freight savings.

## Can you put my logo or a project mark on the spacer mould?
Yes. A raised logo, factory name or project code can be cut into the cavity and appears on every cast spacer; it must be added at tool-making stage, not after. Marking is common for distributors and for large infrastructure projects that need traceability on site.

## 14. What to send for a fast quote

- Application type: spacer block, saddle, bar strip, plum-blossom, round disc, slot insert, test specimen or ballast block.

- Cover thickness, finished spacer dimensions and 1-out-N count.

- Profile drawing, local standard or clear sample photos.

- Order quantity, destination country and whether mixed profile types are needed.

## 15. Avoid vague quote requests

Quotes based only on "spacer mould" without cover thickness, finished dimensions or 1-out-N count usually lead to confusion and wrong samples. For buyers sourcing injection moulding for rebar spacer projects, the shortest useful brief is: application (slab / column / pile cap), cover thickness, finished dimensions, target 1-out-N, quantity and destination country. That is enough for Zhihua to quote a standard catalogue item or review an OEM profile.

## 16. Related guides and moulds

- Why Zhihua moulds last 150+ casting cycles — what the 150-pour rating actually depends on.

- How to demould concrete blocks without breaking them — the handling side of cycle life.

- Plastic vs steel moulds: 5 key factors — why small precision parts run in plastic injection tools.

- Concrete spacer block moulds — the full spacer, cover, saddle and test-specimen catalogue.

- Photovoltaic pier / ballast moulds — commonly shipped with spacers for solar foundation projects.

- Drainage channel moulds — water-management and channel-line infrastructure.

- Paver block moulds — for surface finishing around spacer / rebar cover work.

For OEM spacer block moulds, send a drawing, sample photo or local standard. Zhihua can review feasibility, suggest a mould structure and quote standard catalogue or custom production.

# Guide: Diamond Pattern Drainage Cover Moulds: Anti-Slip Cover Slab Buying Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/diamond-pattern-drainage-cover-moulds-guide

Diamond pattern drainage cover moulds are used to produce textured precast concrete cover slabs for drainage trenches, utility corridors, sidewalks, yards and municipal road edges. The surface pattern is not only decorative; it also helps create a visible anti-slip surface for pedestrian and maintenance areas.
Zhihua keeps the complete product-card images on the related diamond pattern product page so buyers can see the mould picture, Chinese catalogue title, dimensions and orange description notes together.

## 1. Confirm where the cover slab will be used
A cover for a light pedestrian drainage channel is different from a roadside or utility trench cover. Before asking for price, confirm whether the finished concrete slab is for sidewalks, courtyards, drainage trenches, municipal roads, landscaping areas or utility access covers.

## 2. Choose the right surface texture
Diamond pattern texture is useful when the buyer wants a clear anti-slip surface and an easy-to-recognize product style. If the project requires another surface, compare it with Dot Pattern Drainage Cover Moulds, slotted covers or custom-textured cover slabs.

## 3. Check size, thickness and edge form
For cover slab moulds, the critical dimensions are length, width, slab thickness, edge detail and any matching groove or shoulder that fits the drainage channel below. A small drawing or a sample photo with measurements can prevent quotation mistakes.

## 4. Decide catalogue mould or OEM mould
If a standard catalogue size matches your market, catalogue moulds are faster and more economical. If the cover must match a local drainage channel, road authority detail or project drawing, an OEM mould is safer.

- Finished product length, width and thickness

- Photo or drawing showing diamond pattern pattern requirements

- Application and expected load environment

- Quantity, destination country and packing preference

- Logo, letters, numbers or local-standard marks if required
Matching U-drain channel liners? Read the Drainage Channel & U-Drain Cover Buying Guide.

## Need diamond pattern cover slab moulds?
Send your drawing, sample photo or target size. We will review whether a catalogue mould or OEM mould is more practical.
View Product PageRequest a Quote

## Frequently asked questions

## Diamond pattern vs dot pattern — which anti-slip surface should I choose?
Both are anti-slip treads; the difference is visual and project-standard. Dots are round raised studs, the dominant choice on railway tunnel cable trenches; diamonds are interlocking rhombus ribs that read as a continuous directional tread, widely specified on municipal roadside and plaza trenches. Performance is set by slab thickness and reinforcement, not by the tread shape — choose the pattern your drawing or authority standard calls for. Both are moulded from the same PP/ABS tooling.

## What sizes are in the diamond-pattern cover catalogue?
Standard municipal series (6 moulds): 44.4×49.4×3, 54.4×49.4×2.5, 59.4×49.5×6, 49.5×34.5×5, 54×50×5 and 84.4×49.4×3 cm. Heavy railway series (3 moulds): 100×50×8, 126×50×8 and the 148×50×7 diamond Tie Biao railway-standard cover. Dimensions are length × width × thickness in cm; any other size is made to drawing.

## Does the diamond pattern affect the cover's load rating?
No — load comes from slab thickness and concrete reinforcement, not from the tread. The same diamond range includes 2.5-3 cm pedestrian covers and 7-8 cm railway covers. We do not label covers with a D/B load class: that is a property of the reinforced concrete you pour, not of the mould. Tell us the application (sidewalk, road shoulder or trackside) and we confirm the section thickness.

## Does a diamond-pattern cover need a notch or holes?
Only where the trench demands it. A notch is moulded into the edge where a cable or pipe crosses the trench at that cover position — order it with notch width × depth and middle/end position; never cut it on site after casting. Holes are for water-carrying ditches where flow must pass through the slab. The standard diamond catalogue is solid slabs; send your drawing for notched or perforated covers.

## Should I order a catalogue mould or an OEM mould?
If a standard catalogue size matches your market, catalogue moulds are faster and more economical. If the cover must match a local drainage channel, road-authority detail or project drawing — including project marks, logos or a different thickness — an OEM mould made from that drawing is safer and avoids fit mistakes on site.

# Guide: Dot Pattern Drainage Cover Moulds: Textured Cover Slab Buying Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/dot-pattern-drainage-cover-moulds-guide

Dot pattern drainage cover moulds are used to produce textured precast concrete cover slabs for drainage trenches, utility corridors, sidewalks, yards and municipal road edges. The surface pattern is not only decorative; it also helps create a visible anti-slip surface for pedestrian and maintenance areas.
Zhihua keeps the complete product-card images on the related dot pattern product page so buyers can see the mould picture, Chinese catalogue title, dimensions and orange description notes together.

## 1. Confirm where the cover slab will be used
A cover for a light pedestrian drainage channel is different from a roadside or utility trench cover. Before asking for price, confirm whether the finished concrete slab is for sidewalks, courtyards, drainage trenches, municipal roads, landscaping areas or utility access covers.

## 2. Choose the right surface texture
Dot pattern texture is useful when the buyer wants a clear anti-slip surface and an easy-to-recognize product style. If the project requires another surface, compare it with Diamond Pattern Drainage Cover Moulds, slotted covers or custom-textured cover slabs.

## 3. Check size, thickness and edge form
For cover slab moulds, the critical dimensions are length, width, slab thickness, edge detail and any matching groove or shoulder that fits the drainage channel below. A small drawing or a sample photo with measurements can prevent quotation mistakes.

## 4. Decide catalogue mould or OEM mould
If a standard catalogue size matches your market, catalogue moulds are faster and more economical. If the cover must match a local drainage channel, road authority detail or project drawing, an OEM mould is safer.

- Application and expected load environment

## Frequently asked questions

## Why are so many dot-pattern covers used on railway and tunnel cable trenches?
Railway and high-speed-railway tunnel cable trenches run for kilometres beside the track and are walked by maintenance staff, so the cover needs a visible anti-slip surface, a long straight section and a project-standard mark. The catalogue includes the Hangshaotai high-speed-railway tunnel series (42×40×6 up to 79.4×49.4×6 cm, some stamped HST-T2H), Tie Biao railway-standard covers (including an extra-long 120×49×10 slab) and an 80×50×8 high-speed-rail notched cover. Send your railway line or standard and drawing for a matched set.

## Thin 2.5-3 cm covers vs 6-10 cm covers — which do I need?
Thickness follows the load on top, not the pattern. The 2.5-3.2 cm dot covers are pedestrian and maintenance-walkway slabs; the large thin ones are made in ABS so the panel stays straight. The 6-10 cm covers (HST and Tie Biao series, 78×40×7, 80×50×8 and 120×49×10) take trackside/roadside and occasional-vehicle loads. Load class is set by thickness and reinforcement — tell us the application and we confirm the section.

## What do the HST / Tie Biao / project marks on the covers mean?
These are project or standard identifiers cast or printed on the slab. HST marks the Hangzhou-Shaoxing-Taizhou high-speed-railway project (some pieces also carry section codes such as T2H), and Tie Biao means the cover is made to the railway industry standard rather than to a single project. Highway pieces carry authority names such as Guizhou expressway, Baohu, Wenma and the Guiyang southwest ring. We can form your project name, line code, standard number or logo in the mould; send the mark with the drawing.

## Some of these covers have a notch — why?
The edge notch lets a cable or pipe cross the trench at that cover position instead of going under the slab — the cover drops over the crossing line. Quote the notch width × depth and its position (middle of a run or at the end). A notch cut on site after casting breaks the edge and ruins the piece, so it must be moulded in from the start.

## Can you make dot-pattern covers to our railway or expressway drawing?
Yes. Send the finished slab length, width and thickness, the dot or tread requirement, the notch detail if any, the application and expected load environment, plus the project mark or logo. We review whether a catalogue mould matches or whether an OEM mould is required.

# Guide: Drainage Channel Moulds: How to Choose U-Drain and Drainage Cover Moulds
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/drainage-channel-moulds-u-drain-cover-buying-guide

Drainage channel moulds are a high-priority product category for overseas infrastructure buyers because drainage products are used in almost every road, industrial park, municipal and stormwater project. A good mould choice affects the finished concrete unit’s water flow, installation fit, demoulding speed and long-term production cost.

This guide explains how to compare U-drain moulds, drainage cover moulds, ditch slab moulds and catch basin moulds before requesting a quote.

## 1. Start with the finished concrete product

Before discussing mould price, define the finished concrete product clearly. For a U-drain or drainage channel, the most important dimensions are length, outside width, inside waterway width, depth and wall thickness. For a drainage cover, confirm the cover length, width, thickness, slot pattern and whether it must match a specific channel size.

If you only have a sample photo, send a ruler reference or the approximate local market size. Zhihua can review whether a catalogue mould is close enough or whether an OEM mould is better.

## 2. Choose the correct mould family

- U-drain / drainage channel moulds: used for roadside gutters, industrial drainage and irrigation channels.

- Drainage cover moulds: slotted, grating or gap-style covers for stormwater inlets and utility trenches. For finished top-surface covers see also flat stone, notched and handle (recessed-grip) cover moulds — order the channel and cover as a matched pair so the cover seats correctly.

- Ditch slab moulds: flat or shaped concrete slabs used around water ditches, channels or drainage corridors.

- Catch basin components: moulds for drainage collection boxes, covers or related precast parts.

## 3. Check demoulding direction and ribs

Drainage products often include slots, ribs, edges or notches. These details must be designed so the concrete unit can demould cleanly without breaking thin areas. A slightly simpler slot or rib structure can often improve production speed and reduce damage.

## 4. Match the project application

Pedestrian drainage covers, municipal road drainage, heavy industrial drainage and irrigation channels may need different concrete thickness and patterns. Do not choose only by photo. Tell the supplier where the product will be used and whether vehicles will pass over it.

## 5. What to send for a fast quote

- Finished product drawing or clear sample photo

- Length, width, height/depth and wall thickness

- Slot or cover pattern requirements

- Expected order quantity and destination country

- Whether logo, wording or local-standard marking is needed

## 6. Why work with a mould factory directly?

A factory-direct supplier can discuss mould structure, material, packing and mixed-SKU container loading more quickly. For overseas buyers, video factory audit, product photos and export packing support also reduce sourcing risk.

## 7. Patterned cover slab guides

Choosing the top-face pattern? Anti-slip performance and walking comfort differ by pattern. See our focused guides for diamond-pattern anti-slip covers and dot-pattern textured covers, with size, thickness and traffic-load selection notes.

## Need drainage moulds for a project?

Send your drainage channel or cover drawing/photo. We will review the mould structure and reply with a practical quotation plan.

## Which products are included in the drainage mould category?
U-drain and drainage channel moulds, slotted and gap-style drainage cover moulds, ditch slab moulds, side ditch parts and catch basin components. For finished top-surface covers, flat-stone, notched and recessed-grip handle covers are also available.

## Should the channel and the cover be ordered together?
Yes, order them as a matched pair so the cover seats correctly on the channel: the cover length, width and any shoulder or groove must match the U-drain below. A cover chosen only from a photo often does not seat on an existing channel.

## Which dimensions matter most when requesting a quote?
For a U-drain: length, outside width, inside waterway width, depth and wall thickness. For a cover: length, width, thickness, slot pattern and the channel size it must match. If you only have a sample photo, add a ruler reference or the approximate local market size.

Municipal roads, highways, industrial parks, stormwater systems, irrigation channels and drainage improvement projects. Precast factories and contractors serving these markets are the typical buyers, and mixed-SKU container loading is normal.

# Guide: Flat Kerb, Gutter Strip Stone & Apron Slab Moulds Buying Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/flat-kerb-strip-stone-moulds-buying-guide

When buyers talk about “kerbstone moulds” they often mean only the upright road edge stone. But a finished road edge is usually two precast pieces working together: the upright kerb that holds the edge, and a family of flat-laid stones that carry surface water toward the drain and smooth the transition between carriageway and footway. In Chinese these are ping shi (平石, flat stones), tiao shi (条石, strip stones) and the large apron slabs. This guide covers how to order them without the common mistakes.

## 1. The four flat-stone families

- Small square flat stones (8–19 cm). Compact squares for footways, courtyards, patches and borders. Many run as multi-cavity moulds (1-out-5, 1-out-6) to keep high-volume unit cost down. Available in PP and ABS, with plain or chamfered faces.

- Thin veneer / small slabs. Sizes like 18.5 × 18.5 × 0.5 cm and 18.5 × 18.5 × 2 cm, including a dished (concave) ABS version. These are thin wear-course / veneer panels — the 0.5 cm thickness is intentional, not an error.

- Strip stones & 50 cm flat kerb stones. The workhorse road module. Narrow 20 cm class strips run 1-out-2 or 1-out-10; the 50 cm class covers gutter strip stones (8–12 cm wide, deeper), round-top strip kerbs (e.g. 50 × 8 × 19) and flat kerb stones from 50 × 10 × 10 up to 50 × 16 × 18.

- Large apron slabs (71–80 cm). Wide transition panels around drains and crossings — 71.5 × 40, 75 × 25/30/48/49, 78 × 50 — including four-hole drainage slabs, beveled faces and tall standing units up to 79 × 18 × 30.

## 2. Read dimensions the flat-stone way

Dimensions are length × face width × height/thickness. For a genuinely flat-laid stone the third number is small (6–21 cm). If the third number is large (e.g. 79 × 18 × 30 or 75 × 12 × 30), the unit is actually a standing profile even though it sits in the flat-stone product family — confirm with the drawing. A very small third number on a wide panel (0.5–2 cm) means a thin veneer slab, not an undersized stone.

## 3. Flat-laid vs upright — the #1 ordering mistake

Buyers sometimes order flat stones where the section calls for upright kerbs (or vice versa) because both are loosely called “kerb stones”. Check the road cross-section: does the unit lie down (flat stone / ping shi) or stand up (kerbstone / lu yuan shi)? The flat stone's face width sets the drainage apron; the upright kerb's height sets the road-edge containment. Get this wrong and either the water won't sheet to the drain or the edge won't contain traffic.

## 4. Match gutter width and apron width to the drainage design

The narrow gutter strip stone (8–12 cm) sits in the channel and sets how much water the line captures; the wider apron slab (25–50 cm) sets the transition zone back to the footway or road. These widths come straight from the road cross-section and the design rainfall, not from habit. Send the section and we will match standard sizes or quote an OEM profile.

## 5. Cavities change both price and output

“1-out-N” is how many finished pieces a single mould casts per pour. A 1-out-10 strip stone mould makes ten pieces per cycle; a 1-out-2 makes two. More cavities mean a bigger mould but far lower cost and labour per finished stone. When comparing quotes, compare cost per finished stone and pieces per day, not just the mould price.

## 6. PP vs ABS

PP (polypropylene) is the default for plain high-volume flat stones — it flexes under vibration and demoulding and reaches 150+ pour cycles. ABS is chosen where a sharp chamfer, a dished/concave face or a thin crisp arris must stay precise over hundreds of cycles. Several small and 50 cm items are stocked in ABS for exactly this reason.

## 7. Thin veneer slabs and large aprons are both real, and both need care

Thin 0.5–2 cm veneer panels cast fine but demould gently to avoid cracking the thin section. Large 71–80 cm apron slabs are flat panels that gain stiffness from their width and the sub-base; the mould has external stiffening ribs to stay flat. Cast large slabs on a level vibrating table, cure fully, and always store/transport them flat — never on edge.

## 8. Project and road-authority logos

We already produce project-marked units — for example a 75 × 49 × 8 cm apron slab with a Guizhou road-bridge authority mark. Standard, four-hole and beveled slabs can be tooled with your logo from artwork. OEM logo tooling typically takes 10–15 days.

## What to send for a fast quote

- Road cross-section drawing (or clear photo) showing flat stone vs upright kerb

- Finished length, face width and thickness/height of each unit

- Cavity preference for volume items (1-out-2 / 1-out-10)

- Application: gutter channel, apron transition, footway, median or courtyard

- PP or ABS, any logo artwork, quantities and destination port

Browse the full range on our Flat Kerb & Strip Stone Moulds page, together with the complementary kerbstone moulds and drainage channel moulds.

## Have a road cross-section to match?

Send the drawing or a sample photo. We will match standard flat kerb / strip stone sizes or quote an OEM mould with your logo.

Request a Quote
Ask on WhatsApp

## Frequently Asked Questions

## What is a flat kerb stone (ping shi) and where does it go in the road section?
The upright kerbstone (lu yuan shi) stands at the road edge to contain traffic. The flat kerb stone (ping shi, flat stone or side-flat stone) is laid FLAT next to it, between the upright kerb and the carriageway or gutter. It forms the smooth apron that guides surface water into the drain. Gutter strip stones and round-top strip kerbs sit in the same flat-laid line. Most road sections use upright kerbs and flat stones together, which is why they are usually ordered as one family.

## How do I read dimensions like 50 x 15 x 15 cm or 18.5 x 18.5 x 0.5 cm?
Length x width (face width) x height/thickness in centimetres. For a flat-laid stone the last figure is normally small (6-21 cm); a tall unit such as 79 x 18 x 30 is a standing profile. A very thin last figure is not an error: 18.5 x 18.5 x 0.5 and 18.5 x 18.5 x 2 are veneer/wear-course slabs, deliberately thin.

## What do 1-out-2, 1-out-6 and 1-out-10 mean for price and output?
They are the number of finished pieces one mould produces per pour. A 1-out-10 strip-stone mould casts ten small stones in one cycle, so the cost per piece and the labour per piece are much lower on volume jobs. The mould itself is larger. Always compare quotations per finished stone and per daily output, not just per mould.

## Which width of flat or strip stone goes next to a drainage channel?
Use a narrow gutter strip stone (about 8-12 cm wide, often deeper) directly in the channel to carry the water, and wider flat kerb apron slabs (25-50 cm wide) as the transition toward the footway or carriageway. Round-top strip stones give a slightly raised rounded edge in the gutter line. The widths come from your road cross-section, so send the section drawing and we will match the profile.

## Can a 6-8 cm thick apron slab really span 40-50 cm wide?
Yes. These large 71-80 cm apron panels are flat precast slabs, not beams; they gain stiffness from their width and the compacted sub-base beneath them. The plastic mould has external stiffening ribs so it stays flat under vibration and curing. Cast them on a level vibrating table, cure fully, and always store and transport large slabs flat - never on edge, or they can crack under their own weight.

## Should flat kerb and strip stone moulds be PP or ABS?
PP (polypropylene) is the default for plain, high-volume flat stones: it flexes under vibration and demoulding and reaches 150+ pour cycles. Choose ABS where a sharp chamfer, a dished/concave face or a thin crisp arris must stay accurate over many cycles; we stock several small and 50 cm items in ABS. Tell us the profile and we will recommend the grade.

## Can you mould a project or road-authority logo into the slab?
Yes. We already produce project-marked units, including a 75 x 49 x 8 cm apron slab carrying a Guizhou road-bridge authority mark. Standard, four-hole and beveled apron slabs can all be tooled with your logo from artwork. OEM logo tooling takes roughly 10-15 days.

# Guide: Garden & Landscape Concrete Moulds Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/garden-landscape-concrete-moulds-guide

Landscape and garden projects use a surprisingly wide range of precast concrete elements: the paving you walk on, the screen walls that give privacy, and the rings and edges that hold planting beds together. All three are cast in plastic moulds, and all three are chosen mainly on finished size, surface pattern and how the units combine on site.

This guide covers the three families most often bought together: stepping stone and faux stone paving moulds, breeze block and decorative screen block moulds, and tree ring and garden edging moulds.

## 1. Stepping stones and faux stone paving

Stepping stones are the entry point for most garden paving projects. Round discs in Ø20cm, Ø35cm and 50cm are set into lawn or gravel, usually cast 5–6cm thick. Because the mould face carries the finished texture, pattern definition matters more here than raw mould strength.

Faux stone moulds go further: they reproduce irregular natural stone texture in sizes from 5×5cm multi-cavity moulds up to 100×45cm slabs. Matte litchi-texture finishes are popular for patios because they stay slip-resistant when wet. For park and scenic walkways, wood-grain moulds cast 90–200cm strips that imitate timber decking without the maintenance.

Traditional Chinese pattern tiles — lotus, cloud, fret, coin and blessing motifs in 32×32 to 50×50cm — serve courtyard, temple and heritage-style paving. These sell on pattern catalogue depth rather than size range.

- Ask for: finished slab length × width × thickness, plus a photo of the target texture.

- Watch out for: whether units sit on sand, gravel, lawn or a mortar bed — this changes the thickness you need.

- Cost lever: multi-cavity (1-out-9, 1-out-25) moulds cut casting time on small units dramatically.

## 2. Breeze blocks for screen walls and ventilated facades

Breeze blocks — also called decorative screen blocks, ventilation blocks or jali blocks — are perforated concrete units that build screen walls, privacy partitions, ventilated facades, garden walls and balcony infills. They give shade and airflow while carrying a strong architectural pattern, which is why they have come back into fashion in Australia, the US, the Middle East and Southeast Asia.

The dominant format is 20×20×6cm — the most widely specified screen block size, and where pattern choice matters most. 30×30×7cm gives a larger face and builds wall area faster, which suits feature walls. Intermediate and thick formats (25×25×6, 32×32×10, 34×34×6cm) cover square fret designs and structural screens, while 40×40×7cm handles high walls and facade panels.

- Ask for: block face size, thickness, and a photo or drawing of the pattern.

- Watch out for: pattern openness — a very open pattern looks good but weakens the wall and needs reinforcement planning.

- Cost lever: stick to one face size across the wall so a single mould family covers the whole job.

## 3. Tree rings and garden edging

Tree rings (also called tree grates or tree pit surrounds) protect the root zone of street and park trees, hold soil in place, stop pedestrians compacting the pit and give the streetscape a finished edge. Garden edging stones do the same job for planting beds and lawn-to-paving transitions.

The important decision is one-piece ring versus modular set. A fixed decorative ring — sunburst, cast-iron-look, cloud or petal motifs in 50×50 to 64.5×64.5cm — looks best but only fits one pit size. A modular four-piece or eight-piece set uses repeated straight units plus corners, so changing how many straights go per side lets one mould kit build several pit diameters. On multi-size municipal projects that usually wins on total mould cost.

For irregular or large pits, straight, elbow and corner segments from 40cm up to 150cm long let you follow almost any outline.

- Ask for: the finished tree pit opening (inner diameter or clear square) and the surround width.

- Watch out for: whether the ring sits flush with paving or is raised as a kerb — the profile differs.

- Cost lever: modular sets beat fixed rings whenever the project has more than two pit sizes.

## 4. Why these three are usually bought together

A single landscape contract often needs all three: paving for the paths, screen blocks for the boundary or pergola wall, and tree rings for the planted areas. Buying the moulds from one supplier keeps the concrete mix, colour and finish consistent across the site, and lets you consolidate everything into one container.

Mixed-SKU loading is normal for these products. A 20ft container can carry a working set of stepping stone, breeze block and tree ring moulds for a mid-size landscaping operation.

## 5. What to send for a fast quote

For any of the three families, the fastest path to an accurate quote is a photo of the target result plus finished dimensions. Specifically:

- Paving: slab size, thickness, surface pattern photo, and whether multi-cavity is wanted.

- Breeze blocks: block face size, thickness, pattern reference, and total wall area in square metres.

- Tree rings: finished pit opening, surround width and height, flush or raised, and how many pit sizes the project has.

- All: quantity, destination country, and whether patterns or SKUs will be mixed in one shipment.

Zhihua has manufactured precast concrete moulds since 2015 and exports to 30+ countries. Typical mould service life is 150+ pour cycles, and OEM moulds can be produced from drawings, CAD files or sample photos.

# Guide: Hollow Block, Hexagonal Paver & Revetment Block Moulds
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/hollow-block-vs-hexagonal-paver-moulds-guide

Hollow blocks, hexagonal pavers and hollow hexagonal revetment blocks are three of the highest-volume products in precast concrete — and three of the easiest to order incorrectly. Each is measured in a different way, and in each case one parameter quietly controls whether the finished unit works: hole geometry for hollow blocks, thickness for pavers, and wall taper for revetment blocks.

This guide covers all three: hollow block moulds, hexagonal paver moulds and hollow hexagonal revetment block moulds.

## 1. Hollow block moulds: hole geometry decides everything

A hollow block mould casts a masonry unit with internal cores. The cores cut block weight, save concrete, improve insulation and give mortar somewhere to key into. The trade-off is compressive strength, which is why hole shape and the wall thickness between cores are the first two things an engineer checks.

Square holes give the largest void for the least concrete and are the default for boundary walls and partitions. Round holes leave thicker material at the corners, so they hold up better where blocks are handled roughly or where rebar passes through. Angled and arched holes exist mainly for appearance where a block face stays visible, and ventilation blocks push open area as far as it will go for airflow.

Format matters commercially too. 20×20×10cm is the workhorse size and where multi-cavity moulds pay off: a three-in-one ABS mould casts three blocks per pour instead of one. The 30×30×10cm double-sided S30 series is finished on both faces, so blocks can be laid either way round — useful for freestanding walls where both sides are seen.

- Ask for: finished block length × width × height, hole shape, hole count and minimum wall thickness between cores.

- Watch out for: multi-cavity moulds need a flat, level casting bed — an uneven bed produces blocks of inconsistent height across the same pour.

- Cost lever: moving from single-cavity to three-in-one cuts labour per block roughly to a third at the same mould price band.

## 2. Hexagonal paver moulds: measure the side, not the diagonal

Hexagonal pavers interlock on six sides. That spreads wheel load better than a square slab and stops the paving creeping under traffic, which is why hexagons stay standard on pavements, parking aprons and park walkways decades after they were introduced.

The sizing trap is simple and expensive: hexagon pavers are quoted as side length × thickness, not across the corners. A 20×8cm paver has 20cm sides and is 8cm thick — but it measures roughly 40cm diagonally. Buyers who order "40cm hexagons" from a site measurement usually receive units twice the intended size.

Thickness is the load decision, and it is worth being conservative. Use 6cm for footpaths and garden paths, 8–10cm for car parks and light vehicle traffic, and 12–15cm for heavy vehicle aprons, slope surfaces and water-conservancy works. Surface type follows the environment: anti-slip and concave-base faces are specified for wet slopes and drainage surfaces, while chamfered edges reduce spalling where vehicles turn.

One detail that saves real money on site: order matching half-hexagon moulds at the same time. Without them, every paving edge has to be cut from full pavers — slow, wasteful, and it leaves a ragged line along the kerb.

- Ask for: side length and thickness, plus expected traffic load.

- Watch out for: the diagonal-vs-side confusion — always confirm which dimension your drawing refers to.

- Cost lever: half-hexagon edge units cost far less than the labour and breakage of cutting full pavers on site.

## 3. Hollow hexagonal revetment blocks: read the wall taper

Hollow hexagonal revetment blocks are the open-cored units laid across river banks, canal slopes, highway embankments and reservoir edges. The hexagon keeps the mat keyed together against water flow, and the open core is planted with grass or filled with gravel so the slope becomes vegetated erosion control rather than bare concrete.

These blocks are specified as side length × block height, plus wall thickness — and wall thickness is usually written as a range like 6–5cm. That is not a tolerance and not a choice: it is a taper, 6cm at the wide face and 5cm at the narrow face, so the cast block releases cleanly from the mould. Treating it as a tolerance leads to arguments over blocks that were actually made correctly.

Side length 14.5–18cm suits canal linings, garden slopes and low-flow banks. 20cm is the most widely used revetment size, with block heights from 6cm to 30cm depending on the design concrete volume per square metre. 22–25cm is specified for main river banks and high-flow channels. As with pavers, half-hexagon and semi-hollow units finish the mat edge without cutting.

- Ask for: side length, block height, and wall thickness including the taper if specified.

- Watch out for: reading a tapered wall spec as a tolerance range — confirm which face each figure refers to.

- Cost lever: block height drives concrete volume per square metre far more than side length does; check it against the slope design before fixing the mould size.

## 4. Why buyers often order these three together

These families look unrelated but frequently land in the same container. A municipal or water-conservancy contract commonly needs revetment blocks for the slope, hexagonal pavers for the walkway on top of it, and hollow blocks for the boundary or retaining walls around the site. Because all three are plastic moulds in similar size bands, they pack efficiently together and share the same freight.

Mixing families in one order also smooths the tooling spend. Mould cost per design is modest compared with the labour and concrete you will spend using it, so it is usually better to buy a wider set of designs once than to reorder in small batches as each work package starts.

## 5. What to send when asking for a quote

The fastest quotes come from a drawing or a photo with dimensions marked. If neither exists, send these:

- Hollow blocks: block length × width × height, hole shape and count, wall thickness between cores, and your target output per day.

- Hexagonal pavers: side length, thickness, traffic load, paved area, and whether half-hexagon edge units are needed.

- Revetment blocks: side length, block height, wall thickness with taper, slope area, and whether cores are planted or gravel-filled.

- All three: quantity, destination country, and whether mixed designs can share one container.

Typical service life is 150+ pour cycles with normal release-agent use and careful demoulding, and OEM moulds can be produced from drawings or sample photos when a project specification does not match a catalogue size.

## Frequently Asked Questions

## What is the difference between a hollow block and a solid block mould?
A hollow block mould has core formers that create internal voids, so the finished unit is lighter, uses less concrete and gives mortar a mechanical key. A solid block mould produces a fully filled unit with higher compressive strength but more weight and material cost per block.

## How are hexagonal pavers measured?
Hexagonal pavers are specified as side length by thickness. A 20x8cm hexagon paver has 20cm sides and is 8cm thick, which measures about 40cm across the diagonal. Ordering by the across-corners dimension is the most common sizing mistake.

## What does wall thickness 6-5cm mean on a revetment block?
It is a tapered wall: 6cm at the wide face and 5cm at the narrow face. The taper lets the cast block release cleanly from the mould and is standard practice on hollow hexagonal revetment blocks.

## How many blocks can a three-in-one hollow block mould cast?
A three-in-one ABS mould casts three blocks in a single pour, and a two-in-one casts two. Multi-cavity moulds cut labour cost per block significantly but need a flat, level casting bed to keep block heights consistent.

# Guide: How Many Times Can You Reuse a Plastic Concrete Mold?
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/how-many-times-can-you-reuse-a-plastic-concrete-mould

## How Many Times Can You Reuse a Plastic Concrete Mold?

"How many times can I use this mold?" (also spelled "mould" in British English) is the first question most buyers ask — and the number they get from a supplier is almost always the one they want to hear. Real production numbers are much wider than the marketing line: anywhere from 30 pours for a cheap recycled-PP mould to 500+ for a well-made ABS mould treated properly on site. This article explains what determines the count, what to ask for, and how to avoid buying a "500-cycle" mould that cracks at pour 60.

## The short answer, by material

There is no single number because "plastic concrete mould" covers three very different materials. Here is what you should expect in real production, not on a datasheet:

- Recycled or thin-walled PP: 30–100 pours. These are the cheapest moulds on the market, often sold on auction sites or bundled with small orders. Walls are 1–2 mm thick and the resin contains a high percentage of regrind. They work for a one-off job, but they deform and crack quickly.

- Virgin PP (standard production mould): 100–300 pours. This is the mainstream category. A correctly designed PP mould with 2.5–4 mm walls, rib reinforcement and proper use reliably reaches 150+. This is what Zhihua quotes as its standard 150+ cycle rating under normal use.

- ABS: can exceed the standard PP counts (300–500+ under careful on-site handling). ABS is harder, stiffer and holds tighter tolerance, which makes it the right choice for fine-pattern work (breeze blocks, logos) and high-volume production. It costs more up front but can give the lowest cost per pour when treated properly. We quote a conservative rating rather than a best-case lab number.

Steel and fibreglass moulds last much longer (5000+ and 1000+ respectively), but at a higher capital cost. For most precast plants running 100–5000 pieces of a given shape, plastic wins on cost per pour.

## What really determines mould life

Material is only one of five factors. Two identically built PP moulds can last 50 pours or 500 pours depending on how they are used.

## 1. Wall thickness and rib design

A 2 mm wall is fine for a 200 mm paver; it is too thin for a 600 mm manhole cover. The deeper and heavier the part, the more internal pressure wet concrete puts on the mould during vibration, and the more reinforcement is needed. A good manufacturer sizes the wall and ribs to the part, not to a single global thickness. Ask for the wall thickness at the thinnest point — if the answer is "about 2 mm" for a large part, expect trouble.

## 2. Draft angle and corner radius

Concrete shrinks slightly as it cures, which makes it grip the mould. A 1°–2° draft angle (taper) lets the block release cleanly. Zero-draft or reverse-taper walls lock the concrete in, forcing workers to hammer the mould out — and every hammer strike shortens its life. Sharp internal corners are the second killer because stress concentrates there during demoulding. A 2–3 mm radius is a cheap mould modification that dramatically extends life.

## 3. Resin quality: virgin vs recycled

Virgin PP has a predictable melt-flow index, impact strength and UV resistance. Recycled or "mixed" PP varies batch to batch — even if the first delivery is fine, the third may be a different blend. If a quote is 30–40% below the market average, recycled resin is almost always where the money was saved. Ask explicitly: "Is this 100% virgin resin, and which grade?" and get the answer in writing.

## 4. Release agent and cleaning

Concrete that is allowed to bond directly to the plastic tears out micro-particles of the mould surface on every pour. A light coating of release agent (purpose-made form release, mould oil, or even diluted dish soap in an emergency) prevents this. Cleaning between pours with a damp cloth before the residue hardens keeps the draft angle working. Moulds caked with old concrete are effectively working at zero draft — they will crack much sooner.

## 5. Handling, storage and climate

UV radiation from direct sun makes PP brittle in 3–6 months. Stacked moulds should be stored indoors or under a tarp. Demoulding should use a rubber mallet and a plastic or wooden wedge — a steel hammer against a PP mould will crack the wall on the first strike. Cold weather below 0 °C also makes PP more brittle; if you pour outdoors in winter, either store moulds indoors overnight or specify ABS / a cold-impact-grade PP copolymer.

## How to verify a supplier's cycle claim before you order

Any supplier can say "500 cycles". These three questions separate marketing numbers from engineering numbers:

- "Which resin grade is used, and is it 100% virgin?" A real answer sounds like "Virgin PP, grade Yanshan 1100K" (or a named Sinopec / Borouge / LyondellBasell grade). "High-quality PP" or "imported PP" without a grade is not an answer.

- "What is the wall thickness at the thinnest point, and how many ribs?" Ask for a cross-section drawing or a caliper photo. Compare it across two or three suppliers — you will quickly see who is engineering the mould and who is just injection-moulding a shell.

- "Can you show me a mould from a previous customer that has done the claimed number of pours?" A supplier with real 150-cycle moulds on real projects has photos of worn-but-working moulds. If they cannot produce one, the number is a lab test, not a production number.

A good follow-up is to ask what invalidates the warranty. If the warranty says "150 cycles under normal use" but "normal use" excludes steel hammers, no release agent, or outdoor storage, you have just learned the real conditions the number depends on.

## Cost per pour is the number that matters

Buyers often compare mould price per piece when they should be comparing price per pour. The math changes the decision:

- A $5 recycled-PP mould that lasts 50 pours costs $0.10 per pour.

- A $15 virgin-PP mould that lasts 150 pours costs $0.10 per pour.

- A $30 ABS mould that lasts 500 pours costs $0.06 per pour.

Add in the cost of a rejected concrete block (material + labour + disposal) when a mould goes out of tolerance at pour 80, and the "cheap" mould is usually the most expensive one on the yard. For any order above a few hundred pieces, move up one grade of mould and the savings show up in reduced rejection, not just in mould life.

## Quick rule of thumb

If you remember one thing from this article: take a supplier's cycle number, divide by two, and that is a conservative production estimate. A "500-cycle" PP mould will do 250–500 pours depending on your crew and climate. A "500-cycle" ABS mould is the same kind of best-case lab number. If even the half-number is good enough for your order quantity, the mould is correctly specified. If you need every cycle, pay for virgin resin, correct wall thickness, proper release agent and indoor storage — and watch your crew for the first week until the demoulding technique is right.

## Plastic concrete mold life FAQ

## How many times can a typical plastic concrete mold be reused?
A virgin-PP or ABS injection-moulded plastic mold typically lasts 100–300 concrete pours under normal use. Thin or recycled-material molds may only survive 30–100 pours, while well-designed thick-walled virgin-PP molds with rib reinforcement routinely reach 150–300 cycles and well-made ABS molds can exceed these counts when treated carefully.

## Does the shape of the concrete part affect mold life?
Yes. Simple flat slabs and pavers with a good draft angle reach the highest cycle counts. Deep, narrow parts (manhole rings, tall channels), parts with zero draft or undercuts, and parts with sharp internal corners concentrate stress and crack earlier, sometimes cutting life by 30–50%.

## What kills a plastic concrete mold the fastest?
The fastest killers are: using a metal hammer to demold, leaving concrete residue to harden in the mold, no release agent (concrete bonds directly to the plastic), storage in direct sun (UV embrittlement), and pouring concrete that is much hotter than 60 °C. Any one of these can halve mold life.

## Are 500-cycle molds real?
Yes, but only when three things are true: the mold is made from a high-grade virgin resin (usually ABS or a PP copolymer), the wall thickness and rib pattern are engineered for the part's depth and weight, and the customer uses correct release agent, rubber mallet demolding, proper storage and cleaning between pours. A supplier quoting 500+ cycles on a thin cheap PP mold is usually quoting the best-case lab number, not your production-floor number.

## How can I verify a mold's claimed cycle life before ordering?
Ask three things: (1) what resin and grade is used and whether it is virgin or recycled; (2) the as-built wall thickness at the thinnest point; (3) a photo of a mold that has done the claimed number of pours from a previous customer. A supplier who cannot answer those three clearly is likely quoting a marketing number, not an engineering one.

## Need moulds with a cycle count you can verify?

Zhihua uses 100% virgin PP and ABS, names the resin grade on every quote, and ships moulds with documented wall thickness and rib design. Standard PP moulds are rated for 150+ pours under normal use; well-made ABS moulds, treated carefully, can reach higher counts. Send your part drawing or photo and we will recommend the right material for your volume and climate.

## How to Choose the Right Precast Concrete Mould

Selecting the perfect mould for your precast concrete project involves more than just matching dimensions. The right choice affects production quality, cycle life, and overall project cost. This guide covers the critical factors you should consider.

Before selecting a mould, clearly define your project scope:

- Target Market: Municipal, highway, railway, hydraulic?

- Delivery Timeline: When do you need production to start?

## 2. Mould Material Quality

Material selection directly impacts cycle life and dimensional stability. Zhihua uses virgin PP (polypropylene) and ABS resins — never recycled regrind.

Why virgin materials matter:

- Consistent melt flow index (MFI)

- Predictable shrinkage during cooling

- Higher resistance to UV and chemical degradation

- 150+ pour cycles without dimensional drift

## 3. Wall Thickness and Reinforcement

Proper wall thickness ensures mould stability under repeated thermal cycling. Our moulds are designed with:

- Controlled wall thickness for uniform cooling

- Reinforced ribs in stress-prone areas

- CNC-verified draft angles (minimum 1°-3°)

## 4. Supplier Track Record

Request evidence of similar projects:

- Case studies with photos of installed products

- Container loading photos for export orders

- Client references in your target market

- Certifications (ISO, High-Tech Enterprise, Patents)

## 5. After-Sales Support

Mould damage or wear is inevitable. Evaluate the supplier's support policies:

- Response time (we aim for

When evaluating mould suppliers, ask these questions:

- What is the expected cycle life?

## Frequently asked questions

## What should I define before requesting a quote?
Four things: the concrete type (C30/40 standard, high-strength or pigment-dyed), the production volume in pieces per day or month, the target market (municipal, highway, railway or hydraulic), and when production needs to start. This determines mould material, cavity layout and lead time.

## Why does virgin PP or ABS matter versus recycled material?
Virgin resins give a consistent melt flow index, predictable shrinkage during cooling, higher resistance to UV and chemical degradation, and 150+ pour cycles without dimensional drift. Recycled regrind varies batch to batch and typically shows dimensional drift and shorter life.

## What wall thickness and draft details should a quality mould have?
Controlled, uniform wall thickness for even cooling under repeated thermal cycling, reinforcement ribs in stress-prone areas, and CNC-verified draft angles (minimum about 1°–3°) so the concrete releases without breaking thin sections.

## What evidence of track record should I ask a mould factory for?
Case studies with photos of installed products, container-loading photos for export orders, client references in your target market, and certifications such as ISO, High-Tech Enterprise or patents. A sample mould or a video factory audit reduces sourcing risk.

## What after-sales support matters for moulds?
Response time, replacement-cavity availability, repair capability and usage guidance (release agent, demoulding and storage) over WhatsApp or email. Mould wear is inevitable, so the speed of cavity replacement matters more than a nominal warranty.

# Guide: How to Demold Concrete Blocks From Plastic Molds Without Breaking Them
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/how-to-demould-concrete-blocks-without-breaking

## How to Demold Concrete Blocks From Plastic Molds Without Breaking Them

Demolding (also written "demoulding" in British English, or stripping) is where good precast parts get ruined. A chip on an arris, a torn surface, or a broken corner turns a first-quality block into a reject. The good news: 90% of demoulding damage is preventable with the right timing, release agent, vibration and a small change in technique. This is the procedure we walk new customers through when they start using our moulds.

## The four things that have to be right before you lift

Demoulding only works when all four are in place. If even one is off, the block will either stick and break on the way out, or come out too early and slump:

- Concrete has reached stripping strength. For most standard mixes at 20–25 °C that is 24–48 hours and roughly 40–50% of design strength. Thin pavers can be ready in 12–18 hours; large structural pieces need 48–72 hours. Cold weather slows this down — below 10 °C you may need to double the cure time or use heated curing.

- Release agent was applied before pouring. Even smooth PP and ABS benefit from a light coating. Apply it with a sprayer or cloth, then wipe off the excess so there is no puddle in the corners.

- The mould was properly vibrated. Vibration settles the concrete and releases trapped air against the mould wall, which is what gives a clean surface. Under-vibration leaves bug holes that grip the wall; over-vibration segregates the mix.

- The mould interior is clean and undamaged. Old concrete residue, deep scratches or a deformed wall will catch the new block. Inspect moulds between pours.

## Step-by-step demoulding procedure

- Check the cure. Press a thumb into a hidden corner of the concrete. If it leaves a clear impression, wait. If the surface is firm and the edge does not crumble when lightly scraped, you are close.

- Loosen the edges. Run a flexible plastic or rubber spatula around the top rim to break the surface seal. Do not use a screwdriver or steel bar — it gouges both the concrete and the mould.

- Flex the mould wall. Plastic moulds are designed to release by slight flexing. Gently press the side walls outward by hand, working around all four sides. You will hear a faint "pop" as the vacuum seal breaks.

- Invert and tap. Place a soft surface (a rubber mat, a pallet with foam, or a clean sand bed) on the ground. Flip the mould in one smooth motion so the open face is down. Tap the back of the mould with a rubber mallet — never a steel hammer. Start at the centre and work toward the edges.

- Lift straight up. Once the block has dropped onto the soft surface, lift the mould straight up. Do not tilt or rock it; that chips the top edges.

- Inspect and cure. Move the demoulded block to the curing area. For full strength, keep it damp (wet hessian, sprinkler or curing compound) for at least 7 days.

- Clean the mould immediately. While the mould is still warm from the pour, wipe out any residue with a damp cloth. Dried concrete is much harder to remove and shortens mould life.

## Which release agent to use

There are three common options, ranked by result:

- Purpose-made water-based release agent — the best choice. Clean, predictable, does not stain the concrete, and works on both PP and ABS. Apply with a cheap garden sprayer.

- Mould oil / form oil — usually a light mineral oil, sometimes cut with kerosene or diesel. Works well but can leave a slight surface sheen or darken pale concrete.

- Diluted washing-up liquid — acceptable as an emergency option. Mix roughly 1 part dish soap with 10 parts water, spray or wipe on, and pour off any pooling.

Do not use used engine oil, grease or thick petroleum products. They stain concrete, stop subsequent paint or render from adhering, and accelerate degradation of the plastic mould.

## Why concrete sticks — and how to fix each cause

- Sticking in one small area only: usually a missed spot of release agent, or a local scratch / residue patch. Clean and polish that area of the mould after the pour, and re-coat more carefully next time.

- Sticking across the whole face: no release agent, or the concrete was poured onto a mould that was still wet from cleaning. Moulds should be dry before applying release agent.

- Surface tears / pulls out in chunks: demoulded too early — the concrete has not reached handling strength. Wait longer and check cure before stripping.

- Blocks break in half on the way out: either the mix is too dry / low cement content, or the mould has an undercut (a reverse draft) that the concrete has locked into. Moulds for precast should have a 1°–2° draft angle; if a mould has zero draft or a reverse taper, that is a manufacturing defect.

- Corner chipping even though everything else looks right: the block is being dropped onto too hard a surface, or the mould is being rocked as it lifts. Use a rubber / sand landing and lift vertically.

## The five demoulding mistakes that cause most damage

- Using a metal hammer or screwdriver. A steel hammer against a PP mould cracks the wall; a screwdriver chips the concrete edge. Use a rubber mallet and a plastic spatula.

- Skipping the release agent "just once". That is almost always the pour that sticks and ruins a mould.

- Demoulding too early to save time. A block that comes out at 12 hours and slumps is wasted material, labour and mould time. It is cheaper to wait than to re-pour.

- Storing moulds in direct sun. UV makes PP brittle in a few months. Store indoors or under a tarp. Brittle moulds crack during flex demoulding.

- Not cleaning between pours. Built-up residue reduces the effective draft angle, so each successive block sticks a little more until one breaks.

## How mould design affects demoulding

If you are buying new moulds, these design choices make a big difference to your daily rejection rate:

- Draft angle. 1.5° on deep parts (kerbs, channels, manhole sections), 1° on shallow parts (pavers, slabs). Zero-draft and reverse-taper walls are almost impossible to strip without a split mould.

- Corner radius. A 2–3 mm internal radius is far less likely to chip than a sharp 90° corner. Sharp corners look crisp in a catalogue but cost you on site.

- Wall thickness and stiffness. A mould that is too thin flexes unpredictably and distorts over hundreds of pours; one that is too stiff will not release by flexing. A balanced wall with rib reinforcement is the sweet spot — this is what gives our moulds a 150+ pour service life.

- Surface polish. A high-polish interior releases better than a textured one. If your part needs a stone-faced or patterned face, that side is usually demoulded against a separate textured insert rather than the mould wall itself.

## Demolding FAQ

## How long should concrete cure before demoulding?
For standard PP/ABS plastic moulds at 20–25 °C, most blocks, pavers and kerbs can be demoulded 24–48 hours after pouring. Slabs and thin sections may release in 12–18 hours. Large structural pieces need 48–72 hours. The concrete should reach about 40–50% of its design strength before stripping.

## Do I need a release agent for plastic moulds?
Yes. Even smooth PP and ABS benefit from a light release coating. Use a purpose-made water-based concrete release agent, mould oil diluted with kerosene/diesel, or (in a pinch) diluted washing-up liquid. Do not use used motor oil — it stains the concrete and degrades the mould.

## Why is my concrete sticking to the plastic mould?
The usual causes are: no release agent, demoulding too early while the concrete is still plastic, demoulding too late after the concrete has hardened into a monolithic bond, insufficient vibration leaving bug holes that grip the mould wall, or a mould with a damaged / scratched interior that catches the concrete.

## Can I demould concrete the same day I pour it?
Sometimes. Thin pavers and small blocks in warm weather with a fast-cure mix can be stripped 8–12 hours after pour. But same-day demoulding raises the risk of chipping and edge breakage — only do it when the mix is designed for early strength and the ambient temperature is above 20 °C.

## How many times can a plastic concrete mould be reused?
Virgin PP and ABS moulds from Zhihua are rated for 150+ pour cycles with proper use — correct release agent, no metal hammers, storage out of direct sun, and cleaning between pours. Recycled-material moulds may last 50–100 cycles.

## Need moulds that release cleanly pour after pour?

Zhihua moulds are built with balanced draft, reinforced walls and virgin PP/ABS so your stripping rejection rate stays low. Send your drawing or product photo and we will confirm the right draft and wall thickness for your part.

Send Drawing for Quote
