# Guide: Kerbstone & Curbstone Moulds Buying Guide
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/kerbstone-curbstone-moulds-buying-guide

Kerbstone moulds and curbstone moulds are widely used for municipal roads, sidewalks, traffic medians, parking lots, parks, residential communities and landscaping boundaries. For overseas buyers, choosing the right mould starts with the local road profile, not only the product name.

Zhihua supplies kerbstone, curbstone, road curb and side stone moulds for standard catalogue products and OEM profiles from drawings or sample photos.

## 1. Confirm the local kerb profile

Different markets use different words for similar products: kerbstone, curbstone, road curb, side stone, road edge stone or concrete kerb. Before asking for a quote, confirm the finished concrete profile and installation purpose.

- Slope kerbstone moulds: used where a sloped surface is needed for road edges, parking areas or drainage transitions.

- L-type curbstone moulds: common for road edges, sidewalks and boundary applications.

- S-type side stone moulds: often used for medians, separators and local road standards.

- Straight kerb moulds: suitable for long road sections and simple boundary lines.

- Radius kerbstone moulds: needed for curves, corners, islands and turning sections.

## 2. Measure the finished concrete product

For road curb moulds, the critical dimensions are length, height, top width, bottom width, slope angle, radius and chamfer. If your project follows a government or road-authority standard, send the cross-section drawing first.

If only a sample is available, provide clear photos from the front, side and top. Adding a ruler or known-size reference helps the factory judge the dimensions more accurately.

## 3. Straight pieces and radius pieces should match

Many road projects need both straight kerbstones and curved kerbstones. The radius corner piece should match the straight profile, otherwise the line may look inconsistent after installation. When requesting a quote, tell the supplier the curve radius or turning angle.

## 4. How radius kerbs are actually cast

A curved kerb line is not one bent unit. The arc is divided into segments, and each segment is a tapered block — shorter on the inner face than on the outer face — so the pieces close a true arc with even joints. A mould marked R1000 and 1/3, for example, casts one third of a 1-metre-radius arc per piece.

Two rules follow from this:

- One mould equals one radius. If a project has bends at different radii, each needs its own mould.

- Corner pieces must be from the same profile family as the straight runs. A chamfered corner will not line up with a line-profile straight kerb.

Watch how this works in our short video: radius kerb moulds R1000 — how curved kerb lines are cast.

## 5. Choose standard catalogue or OEM moulds

Standard kerbstone moulds can reduce cost and delivery time when the dimensions already fit your market. OEM moulds are better when your local authority has a fixed profile, special chamfer, drainage edge or project-specific radius.

For OEM work, a drawing is best. If there is no drawing, a clear sample photo plus finished dimensions can still support an initial feasibility review.

## 6. Match kerbstones with drainage and paver products

Kerbstone moulds are a strong cross-sell with drainage channel moulds and concrete paver block moulds. Municipal roads, sidewalks and landscaping projects often need road curbs, drainage covers and paving slabs together.

For distributors and construction-material factories, a mixed product line can make the catalogue more complete and increase the chance of repeat orders.

## 7. What to send for a fast quote

- Finished kerbstone length, height, top width and bottom width

- Profile drawing, road-authority standard or clear sample photos

- Type: slope, L-type, S-type, straight, radius or corner piece

- Required radius or turning angle for curved sections

- Application: road edge, median, sidewalk, parking area or landscaping

- Order quantity, destination country and whether mixed profiles are needed

## 8. Reading kerbstone dimensions without mistakes

Two dimension conventions cause most quoting errors:

- Tapered heights like “50 × 35 × 18–7 cm” are not a tolerance. On slope and S-type kerbs the last pair is the height at each end of the same unit — the taper is the drainage fall built into the kerb. Say which end your drawing refers to.

- Corner figures like “30–30” are the outer and inner arc length of one curved piece, not length by width in plan. State the corner angle and confirm it with your straight-run profile.

With a section drawing these ambiguities disappear — that is why we ask for one rather than just a product name.

## 9. Kerbstone, curbstone, side stone: the same product by regional names

Buyers search for the same mould under several names: kerbstone moulds (British English), curbstone molds (American English), road curb moulds, side stone moulds, road edge stone moulds and concrete kerb moulds. They are the same product family. What actually differs between markets is the standard profile — the height, width, chamfer and slope used by local road authorities — so always confirm the cross-section rather than matching on words.

## 10. Avoid vague quote requests

A request such as “send kerbstone mould price” is usually too broad. A useful request includes the profile type, dimensions, quantity and photos. This avoids quoting the wrong mould and helps the supplier check whether a standard item can be used.

## Kerbstone mould FAQ

## Is a kerbstone mould the same as a curbstone mold?
Yes. Kerbstone is British English and curbstone American; mould and mold are the same word spelled differently. Road curb, side stone, road edge stone and concrete kerb also refer to the same product family. Match the cross-section profile rather than the name.

## What does a size like 50 × 35 × 18–7 cm mean?
The last two figures are the height at the two ends of the same unit: 18 cm at the high end and 7 cm at the low end. That taper is the drainage fall built into slope and S-type kerbs, not a tolerance. State which end your drawing dimension refers to.

## How many radius moulds do I need for a curved kerb line?
One mould corresponds to one radius. A curve is cast as tapered segments — for example R1000 divided into thirds — and each segment is shorter on the inner face so joints close evenly. Several radii on one project mean several moulds.

## Can corner pieces be used with any straight kerb?
No. Corner and elbow units must come from the same profile family as the straight runs, or the faces will not align at the joint. Order chamfered, line-profile or curved-angled corners to match the profile you cast.

## Should I choose PP or ABS for kerbstone moulds?
Choose ABS where the top arris is chamfered or sloped and must stay sharp over hundreds of cycles; PP is the economical choice for plain high-volume production. Both give 150+ pour cycles with normal demoulding practice.

## Need kerbstone moulds for a road or landscaping project?
Send your kerb profile drawing, sample photo or dimensions. We can review standard catalogue options or OEM mould feasibility.
View Kerbstone MouldsRequest a Quote

# Guide: Manhole Cover & Shaft Brick Moulds: How to Order a Complete Chamber
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/manhole-cover-and-shaft-brick-moulds-guide

Buyers usually enquire about "manhole moulds" as if it were one product. It is two. The cover and its frame close the top of the chamber; the shaft below is built course by course out of bricks. They are quoted separately, they are measured differently, and the mistakes that cause re-orders are different in each case.

This guide covers both: manhole cover and well frame moulds and shaft ring brick and well wall brick moulds. Every dimension quoted below is read off our own workshop photographs, not taken from a catalogue.

## 1. Cover only, cover plus frame, or frame only?

This single question causes more re-quoting than any other in the category. A cover slab cast on its own will not sit flush unless the seat it drops into was dimensioned to match it. There are three legitimate answers:

- Cover only — the site already has steel frames or existing concrete seats. Measure the seat opening before ordering, because the cover has to be sized to that opening, not to a nominal figure.

- Cover plus frame, as a matched set — two moulds designed together so the clearance is built in. The 50 × 50 cm square set is an example: cover plate and slotted frame, dimensioned against each other.

- Frame only — you are re-seating an existing cover, or capping a shaft. Here the number that matters is the clear opening. Our round frame mould is Ø 68 cm on the outside but gives a Ø 61 cm opening, and it is the 61 that has to match your shaft and your cover.

Getting this wrong is expensive in a way that is easy to underestimate: the concrete is already cast before anyone discovers the cover rocks in its seat.

## 2. Round covers: diameter first, thickness second — and holes are voids, not pitch

Round sewer covers are quoted as diameter × thickness. Ø 80 × 5.5 cm means an 80 cm circle, 5.5 cm deep. Two things follow from that.

First, 5.5 cm is a light-duty section. It suits pedestrian areas, yards and utility access. It is not a roadway cover unless your own concrete design and reinforcement make it one — and that is your engineering decision, not a property of the mould.

Second, when a cover has cast-in drainage holes, the hole dimensions describe the void, not the spacing. On the five-hole Ø 80 cm cover the openings are Ø 22 × 4 and Ø 20 × 3 — those are the sizes of the holes themselves. Buyers occasionally read such figures as a hole pitch and then find the pattern does not match their local standard. If a standard fixes your hole layout, send the drawing: hole geometry is the cheapest thing in the world to change before tooling is cut, and among the most expensive afterwards.

## 3. Shaft ring bricks: one mould equals one diameter

Circular manhole shafts are built from curved bricks. Each mould is cut to a single arc, and that arc is what makes a course close into a true circle. The consequence catches people out: the number of bricks per course is not a choice.

Shaft inner diameterBricks per courseBrick widthCourse height

Ø 70 cm717.5 cm20 cm

Ø 80 cm818.5 cm20 cm

Ø 90 cm9—20 cm

Ø 110 cm1124 cm20 cm

Ø 130 cm (R65)—23.5 cm20 cm

Ø 150 cm (R75)—24 cm20 cm

A Ø 90 cm mould cannot build a Ø 110 cm shaft. The bricks will not meet, and there is no site remedy short of cutting every unit. Projects that mix diameters need one mould per diameter — which is entirely normal, and mixed-SKU shipments are standard for us.

The upside is leverage. One mould is reusable for hundreds of pours, and casting bricks locally removes the freight cost of shipping finished concrete rings, which is where most of the money goes on imported precast chambers.

## 4. The half-metre mistake: inner diameter is not excavation width

Every diameter above is the inner diameter — the clear bore a worker climbs down. Outer diameter is the bore plus twice the wall:

- Ø 110 cm bore + 2 × 24 cm walls ≈ 158 cm outer

- Ø 70 cm bore + 2 × 17.5 cm walls ≈ 105 cm outer

Trench width, shoring and lifting clearance all come off the outer figure. Size the excavation from the bore instead and you are short by nearly half a metre on the large diameters — discovered, invariably, with the digger already on site. Always state which figure your drawing uses.

## 5. Rectangular chambers: straight and corner wall bricks

Not every chamber is round. Valve pits, meter boxes and larger junction chambers are often rectangular, and those are built from straight wall bricks with corner units to turn the corners.

- 30 × 15 × 17.3 cm interlocking brick — tongue 11.5 × 4.5 cm, groove 10.3 × 3.3 cm, so courses key into each other instead of relying on mortar alone for alignment.

- 32 × 18 × 17.3 cm corner brick — turns the corner at the same 17.3 cm course height as the straight unit, so courses stay level around the chamber.

- 40 × 30 × 19 cm brick — a heavier unit for larger chambers and thicker walls.

Keep course heights consistent within one chamber. Mixing a 17.3 cm brick with a 19 cm brick in the same wall forces a packing course somewhere, and that joint becomes the leak path.

## 6. What to send for a quote

Six figures, all from the same drawing, are enough to confirm whether a catalogue mould fits or whether an arc has to be cut new:

- Shaft inner diameter — or chamber length × width if rectangular

- Wall thickness (brick width) your design calls for

- Course height — 20 cm is standard for ring bricks

- Cover size and thickness, and whether the frame is cast too

- Drainage-hole count, size and layout if a standard fixes them

- Number of chambers, destination country, and whether diameters are mixed

A clear photo of the brick or cover you want to reproduce, with dimensions written beside it, is worth more than a paragraph of description.

## Frequently asked questions

## Do I need a frame mould as well as a cover mould?

Only if the frame is being cast in concrete. Where the site already has steel frames or existing concrete seats, the cover mould alone is enough, but the seat opening must be measured first so the cover is dimensioned to drop in. When both parts are cast, order them as a matched set so seat clearance is designed in rather than ground off afterwards.

## How many shaft ring bricks are needed per course?

The mould decides, not the site. A Ø 70 cm shaft takes 7 bricks per course, Ø 80 cm takes 8, Ø 90 cm takes 9 and Ø 110 cm takes 11. Each mould is cut to one arc, so the pieces only close into a true circle at their own diameter.

## Is the quoted diameter the inner or the outer diameter?

Inner — the clear bore of the finished shaft. Outer diameter is the bore plus twice the brick width, so a Ø 110 cm shaft with 24 cm bricks measures about 158 cm outside. Excavation and shoring are sized from the outer figure.

## What load class do concrete covers cast in these moulds achieve?

Load class is a property of the finished concrete, not of the plastic mould. It comes from mix design, reinforcement and slab thickness. A 5.5 or 6 cm cover section is typical for pedestrian and light-utility duty; trafficked covers need a thicker reinforced section designed by the buyer.

## Can ring brick moulds be made for a diameter that is not stocked?

Yes. Supply the inner diameter, wall thickness and course height from one drawing, and the arc and piece count are set so the ring closes exactly. Odd diameters are routine; mismatched figures from different drawings are the only real problem.

## Related pages

- Manhole cover, sewer cover and well frame moulds — square 50 × 50 × 6 cm, rectangular 60 × 40 × 6 cm, round five-hole Ø 80 × 5.5 cm, cover + frame set, Ø 68 cm frame

- Shaft ring brick and well wall brick moulds — Ø 70 to Ø 150 cm ring bricks, straight and corner wall bricks

- Drainage channel moulds — the pipe runs that connect the chambers

- Cable trench moulds — utility trenching in the same networks

Need moulds for a manhole project? Send the shaft drawing or a photo with dimensions on WhatsApp or through the enquiry form. We will confirm the arc, piece count and demoulding before quoting.

# Guide: Photovoltaic Pier Moulds Guide: Solar Support and PV Foundation Bases
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/photovoltaic-pier-moulds-solar-foundation-guide

Buying Guide

## Photovoltaic Pier Moulds Guide: Solar Support and PV Foundation Bases
How to select photovoltaic pier moulds for solar support bases, ground-mounted PV foundations, cable grooves and custom renewable-energy project components.

Published June 14, 2026 · Updated September 3, 2026 · Zhihua Moulds

## What is a photovoltaic pier mould?

A photovoltaic pier (also called a solar pier, PV support base, concrete solar block or, on rooftop projects, a PV ballast block) is the small precast concrete block that a solar panel support structure sits on or bolts to. The mould is the plastic form these blocks are cast in. Because every block in a solar array must share identical dimensions and bolt positions, contractors precast hundreds or thousands of them in reusable plastic moulds rather than pouring in place — faster, cleaner and dimensionally consistent.

Zhihua's catalogue PV pier moulds produce two finished sizes — 30 × 20 × 30 cm and 30 × 30 × 30 cm — in a plain (flat-top) version and a grooved version with a pre-formed slot/cable recess in the top. Beyond these, solar foundation blocks are one of the most commonly customised moulds we make, because foundation geometry is set by the racking system and the site, not by a universal standard.

## Where PV piers are used — three different projects, three different blocks

- Ground-mounted utility & commercial solar farms. Rows of tilted panels on fixed-tilt racking. Each post or racking foot is anchored to a concrete block (or to a driven pile — see below). Blocks need lifting points, bolt pockets that match the racking supplier's hole pattern, and a finish that can sit outdoors for 25+ years.

- Rooftop distributed solar (commercial/industrial roofs). Because you cannot drill through a waterproof roof membrane, arrays are held down by ballast blocks that rely on weight, not penetration. These blocks must be heavy enough for wind uplift but the total roof load must stay under the structure's limit — so the block size and count are an engineering calculation, not a guess.

- Single-axis trackers. Tracker rows rotate and apply cyclic, eccentric loads to their foundations. Tracker foundations are not interchangeable with fixed-tilt blocks; the mould must match the tracker vendor's foundation drawing exactly, and the concrete/steel arrangement is typically vendor-specified.

## Fixed-tilt vs tracker foundations — why the mould differs

Fixed-tilt arrays use static, evenly-loaded blocks: a square or rectangular pier with bolt pockets for the racking column is usually enough, and the loads are predictable vertical and wind forces. Single-axis tracker foundations carry a moving, eccentric load and a torque arm — the block (or pile cap) is sized by the tracker manufacturer for overturning and torsion. A tracker foundation mould is therefore almost always a custom mould from the racking/tracker vendor's foundation drawing, with specific anchor positions, embed plates or anchor-bolt spread. Ordering a generic fixed-tilt block for a tracker row is one of the most common and expensive mismatches we see.

## Ground blocks vs roof ballast blocks — do not treat them as the same product

On the ground, the block's job is to hold the racking down and in position; weight is rarely the limiting factor, and embed plates or cast-in anchor bolts transfer the load. On a roof, the block's entire job is weight (ballast), spread over enough area not to damage the membrane, while keeping total load inside the roof's point-load and overall-load limits. A roof ballast block is often a lower, wider, flatter shape (with a recess to cradle the rail) rather than a tall square pier. If your project is rooftop, tell us the roof allowable load (kg/m²), wind zone and the racking rail section — the block is then sized backwards from the engineering, not chosen from a catalogue.

## What to get exactly right on the drawing (the parts that break projects)

- Bolt / anchor layout. The spacing, thread size (commonly M10–M16 for small blocks, larger for trackers) and projection of the anchor bolts, or the position of cast-in embed plates, must match your racking. A 10 mm bolt-position error means the post does not mount. Send the racking supplier's foundation detail, not just a photo of a block.

- Bolt pockets vs cast-in bolts. A bolt pocket (a recess you set an anchor into later) gives adjustment on site; a cast-in bolt/embed plate is faster to install but must be perfect. The mould is built differently for each.

- Cable grooves. The grooved pier has a pre-formed slot so the string cable can route under or alongside the block without a separate conduit crossing. Confirm the groove width/depth matches your cable bundle.

- Lifting / handling detail. Blocks of 50–200 kg need either a lifting insert, a hand-hole or a shape that can be grabbed. Specify how blocks are placed on site.

- Reinforcement. Larger ballast and tracker blocks may need rebar or wire mesh; the mould must suit reinforced pours and vibration.

## How much concrete, and how many blocks?

A 30 × 30 × 30 cm solid block is roughly 0.027 m³ of concrete — about 60–65 kg at normal 2,300–2,400 kg/m³ reinforced density (a plain, unreinforced mix is a little lighter). The 30 × 20 × 30 cm block is about 0.018 m³, roughly 40–43 kg. Use these only as estimating figures — the real weight follows the actual mix and whether the block is solid or has a recess.

Block count depends on the racking layout (typically one support per column/pier location, spaced per the wind/snow engineering). Customers most often ask us for "how many blocks per MW" — but the answer genuinely varies: fixed-tilt ground arrays, ballasted roofs and trackers each have different support spacing, and soil/wind zones change it. We recommend you count pier locations from your racking layout drawing, add a small breakage allowance, and confirm the weight per block against the site's handling and roof-load limits.

## PP vs ABS for solar pier moulds

Standard square piers in the catalogue sizes cast cleanly in PP (polypropylene), which flexes during demoulding and survives 150+ pour cycles at the lowest cost. ABS is chosen when the block has deep bolt pockets, thin fin walls around recesses, cast-in embed plates (the mould holds rigid inserts that must stay aligned), or the tracker geometry needs stiffer walls that hold tight tolerance over hundreds of casts. We recommend the material once we see the block drawing and production volume.

## Lead time, MOQ and ordering

Catalogue 30×20×30 and 30×30×30 pier moulds (plain and grooved) are standard and ship quickly. Custom bolt patterns, embed-plate moulds and tracker/ballast designs are made to order from your foundation drawing, typically 15–30 days after drawing approval. Mixed-SKU orders are normal (e.g. plain and grooved piers together, or piers plus the cable-trench and drainage moulds a solar site also needs) with no strict MOQ. Send the foundation/racking detail, block dimensions, quantity, destination port and the block weight target for an FOB Ningbo/Shanghai quote.

## Frequently asked questions

## What standard PV pier sizes are in stock?
The two catalogue sizes are 30 × 20 × 30 cm and 30 × 30 × 30 cm, each available plain (flat-top) or grooved (with a pre-formed cable/recess slot). These cover many small and distributed solar projects; utility-scale, roof-ballast and tracker foundations are usually custom.

## Can you cast bolt pockets, anchor plates or cable grooves into the block?
Yes. The mould can form bolt pockets (set anchors on site), cast-in anchor bolts or embed plates (fixed in the pour), lifting points and the top cable groove. These features must be designed into the mould up front — send the racking/foundation drawing with the bolt positions and sizes.

## What is the difference between a fixed-tilt pier and a tracker pier?
Fixed-tilt piers carry static vertical/wind loads and are usually simple square blocks with bolt pockets. Tracker foundations carry rotating, eccentric and torsional loads and are defined exactly by the tracker manufacturer — they are almost always custom moulds from that vendor's foundation drawing and should not be substituted with a generic block.

## How heavy is a 30×30×30 solar pier?
Roughly 60–65 kg at a 2,300–2,400 kg/m³ mix (about 0.027 m³ of concrete). The 30×20×30 block is about 40–43 kg. Actual weight depends on the mix and whether the block is solid or recessed; we quote the mould to your target finished weight.

## How do I size ballast blocks for a rooftop array?
From the engineering, not from a catalogue: provide the roof allowable load (kg/m²), wind zone, panel tilt and the racking rail section. The block must be heavy enough to resist wind uplift while keeping total roof load within the structure's limit. We mould the size the calculation calls for.

## PP or ABS for solar pier moulds?
Plain catalogue blocks cast well in PP (150+ pours, lowest cost). Choose ABS for deep bolt pockets, thin recess walls, cast-in embed plates that must stay aligned, or tracker geometry needing tight tolerance over many casts. We recommend material after seeing the drawing.

## What is the lead time and minimum order?
Catalogue pier moulds are in stock and ship fast; custom bolt patterns, embed-plate and tracker/ballast moulds are 15–30 days after drawing approval. Mixed orders (piers plus cable-trench/drainage moulds) are welcome with no strict MOQ, FOB Ningbo/Shanghai.

# Guide: Plastic vs Steel Moulds: 5 Key Factors
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/plastic-vs-steel-moulds-5-key-factors

## Plastic vs Steel Moulds: 5 Key Factors

Plastic moulds offer significant advantages over steel for many applications. We break down the five critical factors.

## 1. Durability

Plastic: 150+ cycles with proper material quality. No rust or corrosion.

Steel: Can last 1000+ cycles but requires regular maintenance to prevent rust.

## 2. Cost

Plastic: 60-70% cheaper upfront. No maintenance costs.

Steel: Higher initial cost. Regular maintenance and coating renewal required.

## 3. Maintenance

Plastic: Minimal. Clean with mild detergent. No special storage needed.

Steel: Requires rust protection, oiling, and controlled storage environment.

## 4. Production Efficiency

Plastic: Lightweight, easier to handle. Faster cooling cycles.

Steel: Heavy, requires lifting equipment. Slower demoulding.

## 5. ROI Comparison

For most precast applications, plastic moulds deliver higher ROI due to lower total cost of ownership and simpler operations.

## Not Sure Which Material to Choose?

Contact our engineering team for personalized material recommendations based on your specific project.

Get Expert Advice💬 WhatsApp: +86 16621391202

## Frequently asked questions

## How long do plastic moulds last compared with steel?
Injection-moulded PP/ABS moulds deliver 150+ casting cycles with correct release agent, rubber-mallet demoulding and proper storage, and never rust or corrode. Steel moulds can reach 1000+ cycles but need regular rust maintenance and coating renewal.

## How much cheaper are plastic moulds upfront?
Plastic moulds are typically 60–70% cheaper to buy and carry virtually no maintenance cost; steel moulds have a higher initial cost plus ongoing rust protection, oiling and controlled storage.

## Are plastic moulds faster to produce with?
Yes. Plastic moulds are lightweight and easy to handle without lifting equipment, and they cool faster, which shortens each cycle. Steel moulds are heavy, require lifting gear and demould more slowly.

## When does steel still make sense?
For a very long production run of one identical heavy component where the 1000+ cycle life and rigid steel structure justify the higher capital, handling and maintenance cost. For most precast applications — especially multi-SKU and export production — plastic gives a lower total cost of ownership and higher ROI.

## Which plastic material should I choose, PP or ABS?
ABS holds sharper edges and suits thin large panels and profiled faces that take heavy handling; PP is the economical choice for plain high-volume shapes. Both reach 150+ pour cycles under normal use.

# Guide: Power Engineering Concrete Moulds: Cable Trench Coping, Corners and Platform Caps
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/power-engineering-concrete-moulds-guide

Buying Guide

## Power Engineering Concrete Moulds: Cable Trench Coping, Corners and Platform Caps
A practical guide to selecting concrete moulds for power engineering concrete: cable trench and boundary wall coping, corner and curved coping pieces, transformer platform coping, cobblestone combination moulds and ground anchors.

## Frequently asked questions

## How do I read a size like 64–49 × 20 × 6 on a corner coping mould?
The first two numbers are the outer and inner arc length of the same corner piece, not length by width. That part measures 64 cm along its outer face and 49 cm along its inner face, with a 20 cm width and 6 cm height. State clearly which face your drawing dimension follows, otherwise the corner will not close against the straight runs.

## Is a cobblestone combination mould one piece or two?
Two. The A half and B half close together to form the sphere cavities, so they are ordered and counted in sets. We hold 6×10 cm and 10×15 cm versions plus a 10-cavity mould for 8 cm spheres.

## Why are transformer platform copings sold as pairs?
Because the platform corners mirror each other. The 90×20×20 cm and 110×15×10 cm units are marked A (left) and B (right); ordering only one side leaves the opposite corner without a matching cap.

## How do I choose the coping width?
Start from the finished thickness of the trench or boundary wall the coping sits on, then select a width that overhangs evenly on both faces. That is why the same 100 cm length is held in 15, 20, 25 and 34 cm widths. Fix the top profile — flat, single arc, double arc or double-line grooved — before quoting, because it changes the mould itself.

## Should I choose PP or ABS for coping moulds?
ABS holds a sharper edge on grooved and tight double-arc profiles and tolerates more handling on site; PP is the lower-cost choice for plain flat-topped coping produced in high repeat volumes. Typical service life is 150+ pour cycles with either material.

Published June 14, 2026 · Zhihua Moulds

## Where power engineering moulds are used
Power distribution projects, substations, transformer platforms, utility corridors, industrial parks and municipal cable trenches are the main application scenarios. In practice most of the volume is coping — the concrete cap that sits on top of a cable trench wall or a boundary wall — plus the corner pieces needed wherever those walls turn. Buyers need stable finished dimensions, clean demoulding and repeatable production across project quantities.

## Main mould types to compare
Straight coping moulds are the core group, held in lengths of 28.5, 40, 74.5, 75, 80 and 100 cm with widths from 12.5 to 34 cm and heights from 6 to 25 cm. Top profiles vary: plain, strip, single arc, double arc and double-line grooved. Around them sit corner coping moulds (47×25×15, 50×25×15, 64–49×20×6 and 80–80×15×12 cm, including a welded type), transformer platform copings supplied as A/B pairs (90×20×20 and 110×15×10 cm), cobblestone combination moulds, a 42×42×8.3 cm pillar cap, an L-shaped cable trench coping and a 56×28×13 cm ground anchor mould.

## Three specification traps on these moulds
These come up in almost every enquiry, and each one has caused wrong orders.

- “64–49” is not 64 by 49 cm. On corner and curved coping the two numbers are the outer and inner arc length of one and the same piece: 64 cm measured along the outside face, 49 cm along the inside. Read as a rectangle, it produces a mould that will not close against the straight runs. State which face your drawing dimension follows.

- A cobblestone mould is two halves, not one part. These are A+B combination moulds — the A half and the B half close together to form the sphere cavities, so they are quoted and counted in sets. We hold 6×10 cm and 10×15 cm versions plus a 10-cavity mould for 8 cm spheres.

- Transformer platform copings ship as left/right pairs. The 90×20×20 and 110×15×10 cm units are marked A (left) and B (right) because the platform corners mirror each other. One side alone leaves the opposite corner uncapped.

## Getting the coping width right
Coping width follows the finished thickness of the wall it caps, not a catalogue preference. That is exactly why the same 100 cm length is held here in 15, 20, 25 and 34 cm widths. Measure the wall first, then choose the width that overhangs evenly on both faces, and fix the top profile before quoting — flat, single arc, double arc or double-line grooved changes the mould itself, not just the finish. One 100×20×20 cm coping in this range is dimensioned to sit with China Southern Power Grid cover slabs, so if your project follows a specific grid standard, say so up front.

## PP or ABS
Several coping moulds in this range exist in both materials. ABS holds a sharper edge on grooved and tight double-arc profiles and tolerates more handling on site; PP is the lower-cost choice for plain flat-topped coping produced in high repeat volumes. Typical service life is 150+ pour cycles either way. As a rule the mould should match the finished concrete geometry rather than the product name alone, so send drawings, section dimensions and sample photos for feasibility and packing review.

## How to request a quote
Send a component schedule rather than asking for a general price list: for each item give the finished size, the top profile, the quantity, and for corners the angle plus which face the arc length refers to. Add destination country and any local grid standard or marking requirement. For OEM work include a drawing or clear photos from several angles.

# Guide: Rail Transit Precast Concrete Moulds Guide: Railway Infrastructure
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/rail-transit-precast-concrete-moulds-guide

Buying Guide

## Rail Transit Precast Concrete Moulds Guide: Railway Infrastructure
A practical guide to selecting concrete moulds for railway and metro infrastructure components including cable troughs, drainage channels, cover slabs and OEM rail transit parts.

## Frequently asked questions

## Which railway standard do the grid-emblem covers follow?
The grid-pattern covers carry the China Railway emblem (Tie Biao, railway standard) and are used on railway subgrade drainage and cable trenches. Catalogue sizes include 40×32×6.6 cm and 65.4×49.4×6.3 cm; send your project drawing or standard code so we match the exact emblem, tread and dimensions.

## Are the stepped transition cover variants interchangeable?
No. The 85×13×14.3 cm stepped covers come in three step profiles (step 37.5 / 42.5 / 55.5). Each mould produces only one step height, so specify the step profile and the trench height difference rather than ordering by outer size alone.

## What are the fence footing blocks used for?
The 39×22×12 cm and 39×22×12.5 cm footing blocks are precast foundations for high-speed-rail and railway subgrade fence posts. Formed sockets and a drainage opening let the post locate quickly without cast-in-situ concrete; confirm your post section and embedment depth.

## Do you mark a load-bearing class on the cover moulds?
No, and buyers should not request one on a mould. Load capacity is a property of the finished concrete cover — rebar design, concrete grade and slab thickness — not of the plastic mould. We mould the cover dimensions, emblem and tread; structural design follows the project engineering drawing.

## Which material, PP or ABS, is used for rail transit moulds?
Both PP and ABS are available. ABS suits thin large panels that must stay straight and sharp-edged profiles; PP suits plain high-volume components. The choice follows the component geometry and handling on site, and is reviewed from your drawing.

## Can these moulds be made from project drawings?
Yes. Send the finished component size and section drawing, the component type (cable trough, drainage channel, cover slab or utility part), the installation environment, marking or embedded-part requirements, quantity and destination country. We review catalogue matching or OEM feasibility.

Railway lines, metro construction, rail transit stations, cable trough systems, drainage channels, utility corridors, cover slabs and precast infrastructure upgrades

## Main product scope
Railway cable trough moulds, rail drainage channel moulds, concrete cover slab moulds, metro utility component moulds and custom rail transit precast component moulds

# Guide: Slope Protection Concrete Moulds Guide: Revetment Blocks, River Banks and Canal Lining
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/slope-protection-concrete-moulds-guide

Buying Guide

## Slope Protection Concrete Moulds Guide: Revetment Blocks, River Banks and Canal Lining
How to choose slope protection moulds for hexagonal revetment blocks, river bank protection, canal lining, road embankments and ecological concrete blocks.

## Frequently asked questions

## What does a wall thickness marked 6–5 cm on a hollow revetment block mean?
It is a tapered wall: 6 cm at the wide face and 5 cm at the narrow face. The taper lets the cast block release cleanly from the mould and is standard practice on hollow revetment blocks — it is a draft angle, not a tolerance or a defect.

## How do I choose the right hexagonal revetment block size?
Side length 14.5–18 cm suits canal linings and low-flow banks, 20 cm is the most widely used size for river banks and embankments, and 22–25 cm is specified for high-flow channels and main river works. Block height then follows the design concrete volume. Note the hexagon is quoted by side length, not by the diagonal.

## Do you supply half-hexagon blocks for finishing the mat edge?
Yes. Hollow half-hexagon and semi-hollow moulds in 15×20, 17×8, 20×6, 20×8, 20×12, 20×15, 20×40×12 and 25×20 cm let the revetment mat finish at the edge without cutting blocks.

## What is the benefit of hollow ecological slope blocks?
The hollow area supports vegetation or drainage while the concrete frame protects the slope from erosion and interlocks with the neighbouring units. Interlocking and stepped (I-shaped and half-I) blocks add shear keying between units for embankments and river banks.

## What information do you need for a slope block quote?
Send the finished block length, width, thickness and opening size, the block type (hexagonal, hollow, interlocking, grass-planting, river-bank or canal type), the application, any logo or pattern requirement, quantity and destination country. Mixed-size packing can be arranged based on quantity and mould size.

# Guide: Why Zhihua Moulds Last 150+ Casting Cycles
URL: https://zhihuamoulds.com/blog/why-zhihua-moulds-last-300-plus-casting-cycles

## Why Zhihua Moulds Last 150+ Casting Cycles

Why 150+ pours under normal use is our real, verifiable number — from virgin PP/ABS materials to controlled wall thickness.

## The 150+ Cycle Standard

Under normal use — correct release agent, rubber-mallet demoulding and proper storage — our moulds reliably deliver 150+ casting cycles. This isn't marketing hype — it's the result of deliberate engineering and material choices:

- Virgin Materials Only: We use virgin PP (polypropylene) and ABS resins, never recycled regrind.

- Controlled Wall Thickness: CNC-verified uniform walls ensure consistent cooling and minimal stress.

- Reinforced Design: Strategic ribs in stress-prone areas prevent deformation.

- Quality Testing: Every batch undergoes melt flow index and density testing.

## What This Means for You

Cost Savings: Get the full value of every mould — a typical project needs far fewer replacements.

Consistent Quality: No dimensional drift means consistent product dimensions throughout the mould's life.

Reduced Downtime: Fewer mould changes mean more production time.

## Frequently asked questions

## How many times can one Zhihua mould be reused?
Under normal use — correct release agent, rubber-mallet demoulding and proper storage — the moulds reliably deliver 150+ concrete casting cycles. That is the conservative, verifiable figure we quote rather than a theoretical maximum.

## What makes a mould reach 150+ cycles?
Four factors: virgin PP or ABS resin only (never recycled regrind), CNC-verified uniform wall thickness for even cooling, reinforcement ribs in stress-prone areas to prevent deformation, and batch testing of melt flow index and density.

## What reduces a mould's cycle life in practice?
Skipping release agent, prying or hammering instead of rubber-mallet tapping, storing moulds in direct sun or stacked without support, and using concrete or vibration practice outside the design. Dimensional drift across batches is the usual first sign of a worn mould.

## What does 150+ cycles mean for project cost?
Fewer replacement moulds over the run, consistent finished dimensions across the mould's life (no drift), and less downtime spent changing moulds — so the cost per finished concrete piece drops compared with short-life tooling.

## How can I verify the quality before ordering in volume?
Request a sample mould or a video factory audit to see the wall thickness, rib layout and QC process, and ask for MFI/density batch test records. Factory visits to the Jiaxing/Haiyan facility can be arranged through sales.
